Words you will see everywhere

TermWhat it means in plain English
Ethical hackingBreaking into systems with permission to find weak spots before criminals do
NetworkComputers connected so they can send data to each other
IP addressA computer's postal address on a network (e.g. 192.168.1.10)
PortA numbered "door" on a computer; each service (web, email) listens behind its own door
PacketA small chunk of data sent across a network, like one envelope in a big mailing
ProtocolAn agreed set of rules for how computers talk (TCP, UDP, HTTP)
VulnerabilityA weakness that an attacker could use
ExploitThe actual trick or code that uses a vulnerability
EncryptionScrambling data so only someone with the key can read it
HashA fixed-size "fingerprint" of data; you can't turn it back into the original

How the weeks fit together

The course builds in six stages, and each one needs the one before it. If a week feels hard, the gap is often in an earlier stage.

  1. Weeks 1–3 — Networking foundations. Packets, TCP/IP, addresses and routing: how data actually moves. You can't attack what you don't understand, so everything rests on this.
  2. Weeks 4–5 — Finding targets. Reconnaissance and scanning with NMAP, then spotting weaknesses, cracking passwords and recognising malware.
  3. Weeks 6–7 — Cryptography. The defensive core: keeping data secret (encryption) and trustworthy (hashes, signatures, TLS).
  4. Weeks 8–9 — More attacks. Steganography, biometrics, denial of service, sniffing and social engineering.
  5. Week 10 — Hardware security. Attacks on the chip itself, where even perfect maths can leak a secret.
  6. Weeks 11–12 — Web attacks and tools. Metasploit, SQL injection and XSS, then a final deep dive on NMAP and Wireshark.

The single idea behind it all: ethical hacking is understanding how systems work well enough to find their weak points, so they can be fixed, always with permission and within the law.

topics.title: Ethical hacking and networking basics
topics.intro: Lectures 1–5. The big idea: an ethical hacker attacks systems with permission to find weak spots first, and you can't attack a network until you understand how data moves through one.
topics.html:
What ethical hacking is

Ethical hacking means finding the weaknesses in computers and networks by thinking and acting like a criminal hacker, but with the owner's permission. Other names for it: penetration testing ("pen testing"), intrusion testing, red teaming.

TermPlain meaning
Penetration testA legal attempt to break in. The tester only reports what they found
Security testGoes further: also reviews the company's security policies and suggests fixes
HackingOriginally just "showing computer skill"
CrackingActually breaking security on software or systems
SpoofingFaking where a packet came from (a fake sender IP address)
Denial of Service (DoS)Flooding a computer with traffic until it can't answer real users
Port scanningChecking which "doors" (ports) on a computer are open

The CIA Triad is the three things security protects:

  • Confidentiality: only the right people can read it.
  • Integrity: nobody can change it without being noticed.
  • Availability: it works when you need it.

How attackers get in, and what they do once inside

  • Front door: guessing or stealing passwords.
  • Back door: a hidden entrance, often left behind by developers for testing.
  • Trojan horse: a harmful program hidden inside something you download. Many quietly install a back door.
  • Software vulnerabilities: known bugs. Companies publish fixes (patches), and attackers target anyone who hasn't installed them.

Once inside, an attacker may edit the logs to hide their tracks, steal or change files, install a back door to return later, or use the machine to attack others.

Types of tester

  • Script kiddies ("packet monkeys"): beginners who copy other people's tools without understanding them.
  • Professional testers: write their own scripts (Python, C, Perl, JavaScript, SQL and more).

The three testing models

ModelWhat the tester is toldLike...
White boxEverything: network layout, technology, can interview staffGetting the building's blueprints
Black boxNothing; finds it all out themselvesA real outside attacker
Gray boxSome informationSomewhere in between

A tiger box is a laptop loaded with operating systems and hacking tools for testing.

Staying legal

  • Accessing a computer without permission is illegal, as is spreading viruses or worms and running DoS attacks.
  • Laws differ by country and change fast. Even owning some tools can be illegal in some places.
  • A good tester needs network knowledge, people skills, an understanding of the law, and skill with the tools.

Networks: LAN vs WAN

A computer network is just computers connected so they can talk and share resources.

LAN (Local Area Network)WAN (Wide Area Network)
CoversA room, building or campusCities, countries, continents
SpeedFasterSlower
CostCheaperMore expensive

How data travels: circuit vs packet switching

Circuit switching works like an old phone call. A dedicated path is reserved before talking starts, and nobody else can use it.

  1. Set up the connection.
  2. Send the data at full speed.
  3. Tear the connection down.

The downsides: there's a delay to set up, and the line sits wasted during quiet moments. That's fine for voice, but bad for computer data, which comes in bursts.

Packet switching works like the postal system and is what the internet uses.

  • A message is chopped into small packets, each with a header (a label holding the addresses).
  • Links are shared by everyone, so they're used efficiently.
  • Each router uses store-and-forward: it receives the whole packet, checks its routing table, and passes it on.

Packet switching comes in two styles:

Virtual circuitDatagram
Route chosenOnce, before sendingSeparately for every packet
Packets takeThe same pathPossibly different paths
AnalogyTelephone systemPostal system
ProblemsSetup delayPackets can arrive out of order, get lost or duplicated
StrengthOrderlyNo setup delay; can route around broken links

Three kinds of delay:

  • Propagation delay: time for the signal to travel along the wire.
  • Transmission time: time to push all the packet's bits onto the wire (packet size ÷ link speed).
  • Processing delay: time a router spends handling the packet.

The layer models: OSI and TCP/IP

Networking is split into layers so each one can be designed and changed separately. Each layer only talks to the ones directly above and below it.

OSI layer (7)JobTCP/IP layer (4)
7 ApplicationPrograms you use (web, email)Application
6 PresentationData format and translationApplication
5 SessionManages conversationsApplication
4 TransportReliable end-to-end delivery (TCP, UDP)Transport
3 NetworkAddressing and routing (IP)Network
2 Data linkFrames between neighbours; MAC addressesData link
1 PhysicalRaw bits on the wireData link

Memory trick, from layer 1 up: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

Devices and their layers:

  • Hub: extends a LAN; just repeats everything everywhere.
  • Bridge / layer-2 switch: connects LANs, using MAC addresses (data link layer).
  • Router / layer-3 switch: connects different networks, using IP addresses (network layer).

The TCP/IP family

TCP/IP is the set of protocols the whole internet runs on. It started in the 1970s, funded by the US military's ARPA. It uses datagrams, so each packet travels independently.

ProtocolJob
IPMoves packets from source to destination. Unreliable: packets can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order
TCPReliable and connection-based. Splits messages into packets, reassembles them, and resends lost ones
UDPSimple, fast, no guarantees. Good for small messages like DNS lookups
ARPFinds the MAC (hardware) address for an IP address
RARPThe reverse: finds the IP address for a MAC address
ICMPError and status messages (this is what ping uses)
IGMPTells routers which multicast groups a device has joined

Three kinds of address:

  • Port number: 16 bits; picks the program on the computer.
  • IP address: 32 bits; picks the computer on the internet.
  • MAC address: 48 bits; the hardware ID of the network card.

Encapsulation: envelopes inside envelopes

As data goes down the layers, each one wraps it in its own header. As it comes up at the other end, each header is removed.

Example: a file transfer sends 200 bytes of data.

  1. The application adds its header (TFTP).
  2. The transport layer adds a UDP header.
  3. The network layer adds an IP header.
  4. The data link layer adds an Ethernet header and trailer, making an Ethernet frame.

Inside an IP packet header

The IP header is the "label" on every packet: at least 20 bytes, at most 60.

FieldSizeWhat it does
VER4 bitsIP version (usually 4)
HLEN4 bitsHeader length, counted in 4-byte chunks (5 = 20 bytes, 15 = 60 bytes)
Service type8 bitsPriority
Total length16 bitsWhole packet size in bytes (max 65,535)
Identification, Flags, Fragment offsetUsed when a packet is split into fragments (Week 2)
Time to Live (TTL)8 bitsCountdown; minus 1 at each router; at 0 the packet is dropped. Stops endless loops
Protocol8 bitsWhat's inside: TCP, UDP, ...
Header checksum16 bitsError check on the header only
Source / Destination IP32 bits eachSender and receiver addresses
OptionsvariableExtras, e.g. source routing

HLEN maths: header bytes = HLEN × 4. For example, HLEN 5 = 20 bytes, and 224 bits = 28 bytes = HLEN 7.

Seeing packets yourself: packet sniffers such as Wireshark, tcpdump, Windump and Tshark let you watch real packets and their headers.

🎯 What Assignment 1 tests

  • The CIA triad, and the white / black / gray box models.
  • Packet switching vs circuit switching.
  • Which OSI layer does what (especially the data link layer).
  • Delay maths: total time = transmission time + propagation delay.
  • Minimum TCP header (20 bytes), TTL, the HLEN calculation, MAC address size (48 bits).

topics.title: IP addressing, TCP/UDP and subnetting
topics.intro: Lectures 6–10. This week is about addresses, ports, and how to read packet headers. It has more maths than any other week, but every calculation follows one of a few patterns, and they're all worked through below.
topics.html:
Fragmentation: cutting big packets into pieces

Every link has a maximum packet size, the MTU (Maximum Transfer Unit). When a packet is bigger than the next link's MTU, a router cuts it into fragments. Each fragment travels as its own IP packet with its own header.

There are two ways to put the pieces back together:

TransparentNon-transparent (what IP uses)
Reassembled whereAt the exit router of that networkOnly at the final destination
DownsideAll pieces must leave through the same router; may be cut and rejoined many timesMore overhead: every piece carries a 20+ byte header
UpsideLater networks never know it happenedPieces can take different routes, so throughput is higher

The three header fields for fragments:

  • Identification (16 bits): an ID number shared by all pieces of the same original packet.
  • Fragment offset (13 bits): where this piece starts in the original, counted in units of 8 bytes.
  • Flags:
    • D (Don't fragment): if 1, routers may not cut this packet. If it's too big, it's dropped and an error is sent back.
    • M (More fragments): 1 = more pieces follow; 0 = this is the last piece.

Reading a fragment:

MOffsetMeans
00Not fragmented at all
10First piece
1> 0A middle piece
0> 0Last piece

Worked example (from the slides): 1000 bytes of data, MTU 620 bytes.

  1. Room for data per piece = 620 − 20 (header) = 600 bytes. 600 is a multiple of 8, so it can be used as is.
  2. Piece 1: 600 bytes, offset 0, M = 1.
  3. Piece 2: the remaining 400 bytes, offset 600 ÷ 8 = 75, M = 0.

If a later link has an even smaller MTU, those pieces are cut again. The offsets still count from the start of the original packet.

IP addresses

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers (0–255) separated by dots. This is called dotted-decimal.

Example: 01000010 10001000 00110000 01111110 = 66.134.48.126

Every address has two parts:

  • Network number: which network. Assigned by a central authority. Routers only look at this part.
  • Host number: which device on that network. Assigned by the local admin.

The old class system ("classful" addressing)

The first few bits decide the class:

ClassFirst numberDefault maskNetworksHosts per networkUse
A0–127255.0.0.0 (/8)12716,777,214Huge organisations
B128–191255.255.0.0 (/16)16,38365,534Medium
C192–223255.255.255.0 (/24)2,097,151254Small
D224–239———Multicast (one-to-many)
E240–255———Reserved

Hosts are always 2host bits − 2, because two addresses are taken (see below).

Special addresses to memorise

AddressMeaning
10.x.x.x, 172.16–172.31.x.x, 192.168.x.xPrivate: inside homes and offices, never on the public internet
127.x.x.xLoopback: "this computer itself" (127.0.0.1)
0.0.0.0Default network / default route
255.255.255.255Limited broadcast: everyone on my local network
First address of a network (e.g. 118.0.0.0)The network address: the network's name
Last address of a network (e.g. 118.255.255.255)The broadcast address: everyone on that network

TCP and UDP: the transport layer

Both sit on top of IP, and programs use them to send data.

TCPUDP
ConnectionSet up first (handshake)None, just send
Reliable?Yes: numbers every byte, acknowledges, resends lost data, reordersNo
ExtrasFlow control, full-duplex (both directions at once)Only a checksum and port numbers
Header20–60 bytes8 bytes
Good forWeb, email, file transferDNS lookups, video, games

Ports: which program gets the data

One computer runs many programs at once. A port number (16 bits, so 0–65,535) says which program a packet is for, like a flat number in a building whose street address is the IP.

  • Well-known ports (1–1023): fixed for standard services, e.g. FTP 21, SMTP 25. Listed in /etc/services on Linux.
  • Ephemeral ports: temporary numbers a client picks for itself, so the server knows where to reply.

A unique connection is identified by 5 values, called an association: {protocol, local IP, local port, remote IP, remote port}. For example, {TCP, 144.16.192.5, 1785, 144.16.202.57, 21}.

The TCP header

FieldSizeJob
Source port / Destination port16 bits eachWhich programs at each end
Sequence number32 bitsNumber of the first byte in this segment, used to put data back in order
Acknowledgement number32 bits"Next byte I expect from you"
HLEN4 bitsHeader length in 4-byte chunks
Flags6 bitsSee below
Window16 bitsHow much more data the sender may send before waiting (0 = stop)
Checksum16 bitsError check over the whole segment
Urgent pointer16 bitsWhere urgent data ends

The six flags:

  • SYN = 1, ACK = 0: "I want to connect" (request).
  • SYN = 1, ACK = 1: "OK, connection accepted" (confirmation).
  • FIN: "I'm done sending" (polite close).
  • RST: reset or reject a connection (abrupt).
  • URG: urgent data inside.
  • PSH: push this data to the program now.

The three-way handshake

  1. Client → Server: SYN ("can we talk?")
  2. Server → Client: SYN + ACK ("yes, can you hear me?")
  3. Client → Server: ACK ("yes, let's go")

Why hackers care: if an attacker sends lots of SYNs and never sends step 3, the server holds many half-open connections. Its connection table fills up and real users get refused. This is the SYN flood DoS attack (Weeks 8–9).

The UDP header (8 bytes)

Source port, destination port, length, checksum: four fields of 2 bytes each. The checksum is optional (0 = not used).

Subnetting: splitting a network into smaller ones

A subnet mask says which bits of an address are the network part: 1s for network, 0s for host.

To find the network an address belongs to, AND the address with the mask, bit by bit (1 AND 1 = 1, anything else = 0).

Example: 144.16.72.57 with mask 255.255.192.0

  1. The first two numbers keep their value: 144.16
  2. Third number: 72 = 01001000, 192 = 11000000 → AND = 01000000 = 64
  3. Fourth number: anything AND 0 = 0
  4. Network address = 144.16.64.0

Moving the mask further right "borrows" host bits to make more, smaller subnets. For example, putting 255.255.0.0 on the class A network 10.0.0.0 gives 256 subnets of 65,534 hosts each.

CIDR: the modern way

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) drops the A/B/C classes. You write the address, then a slash and the number of network bits, e.g. 144.16.192.57/18.

PrefixMaskAddressesUsable hosts
/8255.0.0.016,777,21616,777,214
/16255.255.0.065,53665,534
/20255.255.240.04,0964,094
/24255.255.255.0256254
/25255.255.255.128128126
/26255.255.255.1926462
/27255.255.255.2243230
/28255.255.255.2401614
/29255.255.255.24886

The formula: addresses = 232 − prefix; usable hosts = that − 2.

CIDR rules:

  • A block's size is always a power of 2.
  • A block's first address must be divisible by its size.

Example: 144.16.192.24/29 means 32 − 29 = 3 host bits = 8 addresses, so the block runs 144.16.192.24 to .31.

VLSM: subnets of different sizes

VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masks) lets one network be split into subnets of different sizes. This wastes fewer addresses.

Example: the network 192.203.17.0/24 must serve departments of 110, 45 and 50 hosts. Equal-sized subnets can't do it. With VLSM:

  1. Split with /25 into two halves of 128: .0–.127 (for the 110 hosts) and .128–.255.
  2. Split the second half with /26 into two of 64: .128–.191 (45 hosts) and .192–.255 (50 hosts).

🎯 What Assignment 2 tests

  • Reading the first byte of an IP header: version + HLEN → header size → options size.
  • TCP flags (SYN, ACK, FIN vs RST, URG).
  • Broadcast vs network addresses, and the private ranges.
  • Fragment flags (M, offset, DF).
  • Well-known ports; CIDR /26 → mask 192.
  • Data bytes = total length − HLEN × 4; UDP header = 8 bytes.

topics.title: Routing and IPv6
topics.intro: Lectures 11–15. This week answers one question: how does a router decide where to send a packet? It covers routing tables, the protocols routers use to share routes (RIP, OSPF, BGP), and IPv6, the newer version of IP.
topics.html:
Delivering packets

IP is connectionless: there's no route set up in advance, and every packet is routed on its own.

  • Direct delivery: sender and receiver are on the same network, so no router is needed. This also covers the final hop, from the last router to the host.
  • Indirect delivery: the destination is on another network, so the packet hops from router to router until it reaches that network.

Routing tables

Every router has a routing table: a list of "to reach X, send it out of door Y".

MethodThe table storesLike...
Next-hopOnly the next router, not the whole pathAsking for directions one junction at a time
Network-specificOne entry per destination network, not per host"All of Mumbai: go via this road"
Host-specificAn entry for one particular computerA special rule for one house
Default"If nothing else matches, send it here" (0.0.0.0)"Not sure? Ask the main post office"

Tables can be static (typed in by hand, never changes) or dynamic (updated automatically by protocols like RIP, OSPF, BGP).

Columns in a routing table: mask, destination, next hop, interface (which port to send from), and flags:

FlagMeaning
URoute is Up
GGoes via a Gateway (the destination is on another network)
HHost-specific route (a single computer)
DAdded by a reDirect message
MModified by a redirect

See your own routing table: netstat -r (Linux) or route print (Windows).

How a router picks a row: longest match wins

For each row, the router ANDs the destination address with the row's mask. If the result equals that row's destination, the row matches. When several rows match, it picks the most specific one (longest mask). If nothing matches, it uses the default route.

Worked example (from Lecture 15):

DestinationMaskInterface
128.35.57.0255.255.255.0eth0
128.35.57.0255.255.255.128eth1
192.112.17.25255.255.255.255eth2
default0.0.0.0eth3
  • 128.35.57.16: matches both of the first two rows. The /25 row (covering .0–.127) is more specific, so it goes out eth1.
  • 192.112.17.10: row 3 is only for the single host .25, and nothing else matches, so it goes out the default, eth3.

Routing protocols

An autonomous system (AS) is a group of networks and routers run by one organisation, such as an ISP. Each has its own AS number.

Interior (inside one AS)Exterior (between ASes)
ProtocolsRIP, OSPFBGP

RIP (Routing Information Protocol)

  • Distance vector: the "distance" is just the number of hops (routers) to the destination.
  • Each router learns routes from its neighbours' tables.
  • Problems:
    • Slow to notice changes in big networks.
    • Routing loops, including the count-to-infinity problem, where routers keep raising each other's distance to a dead route.
    • Updates use a lot of bandwidth.

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)

  • Link state: every router builds a full map of the AS and works out the cheapest path itself, using Dijkstra's algorithm.
  • "Cost" is configurable: delay, speed, money, and so on.
  • Routers send Hello packets every 10 seconds. No Hello for 40 seconds means the neighbour is treated as down.
  • Its five packet types:
    1. Hello: is my neighbour alive?
    2. Database Description: sync maps at the start.
    3. Link State Request: "send me this piece of the map".
    4. Link State Update: the map info itself (link state advertisements, LSAs).
    5. Link State Acknowledgement: "got it".
  • Messages can be authenticated (cleartext or MD5).

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)

  • The exterior protocol that connects the whole internet together.
  • Runs over TCP port 179. Two routers talking BGP are called peers.
  • Like a distance vector protocol, but it shares complete routes, not just hop counts.
  • At first peers swap whole tables; after that, only changes.
  • Its four message types:
    1. Open: start a neighbour connection.
    2. Update: announce or withdraw a route.
    3. Keepalive: "still here".
    4. Notification: report an error.
  • ISPs run BGP. Most companies don't; they just set a default route to their ISP.

IPv6

IPv4's 32-bit addresses have run out, and it handles real-time traffic like video poorly. IPv6 fixes this.

IPv4IPv6
Address size32 bits128 bits
Written asDotted decimal: 192.168.1.1Colon hexadecimal: 7BD6:3DC:FFFF:0:0:2D:F321:FFFF
Base header20–60 bytes (variable)40 bytes, fixed, plus optional extension headers
Address classesA, B, C, D, ENone; uses prefix lengths
Loop protectionTTLHop Limit (8 bits)
FragmentationRouters may fragmentOnly the sender fragments (fragment extension header)

Shortening IPv6 addresses: one run of zero groups can be replaced by ::. For example, 7BD6:0:0:0:0:0:0:B6 → 7BD6::B6.

The base header fields:

  • Version (= 6)
  • Priority (8 bits)
  • Flow label (20 bits): for traffic that needs guaranteed performance.
  • Payload length
  • Next header: what comes next (an extension header, TCP or UDP).
  • Hop limit
  • Source and destination addresses: 128 bits each.

Extension headers are chained together through "next header": routing, hop-by-hop options, fragment, and authentication.

Three address types:

  • Unicast: one computer.
  • Multicast: every member of a group.
  • Anycast: the nearest one of a group. This is new in IPv6.

Moving from IPv4 to IPv6:

  • Dual stack: devices run both versions.
  • Tunnelling: IPv6 packets are wrapped inside IPv4 packets to cross IPv4-only networks.
  • Header translation: convert between the two formats.

🎯 What Assignment 3 tests

  • Connectionless routing (each packet independent, paths may differ).
  • Direct vs indirect delivery.
  • The H flag; OSPF Hello packets; broadcast addresses.
  • Interior (RIP, OSPF) vs exterior (BGP); the default route 0.0.0.0.
  • IPv6 facts: no classes, fixed 40-byte header, 8-bit hop limit.
  • Usable hosts in a /20 = 2¹² − 2 = 4094.

topics.title: Lab setup, information gathering and NMAP
topics.intro: Lectures 16–20. This is where the course turns hands-on: you build a safe practice lab, learn to gather information about a target, and meet NMAP, the tool used more than any other in this course.
topics.html:
The practice lab

Golden rule: hacking any machine you don't own or have permission to test is illegal. All practice happens on your own virtual machines, with your firewall kept on.

PartWhat it isExamples
HypervisorSoftware that runs "pretend computers" (virtual machines) inside your real one, sharing its CPU, memory, disk and networkVirtualBox (used in the course), VMware
Attacker machineA Linux packed with hacking toolsKali Linux (recommended), Parrot Security, BackBox
Victim machineDeliberately insecure systems for target practiceMetasploitable 2 (Linux), Metasploitable 3 (Windows), old Windows XP/7

You need about 4 GB RAM and 30–40 GB of disk. A low-power alternative is "Live" Kali running from a USB stick.

VirtualBox network modes:

  • NAT (the default): VMs sit hidden behind your computer. They all get the same private IP and can reach the internet, but outsiders can't reach them.
  • Bridged adapter: VMs join your real network like separate computers. Use this when the attacker VM needs to reach the victim VM or your host.

Reconnaissance: information gathering

Reconnaissance ("recon") is collecting as much information as possible about a target before attacking. It's always the first step.

What you're looking for:

  • Network info: domain names, IP addresses, running services.
  • System info: usernames, system names, architecture.
  • Organisation info: employees, locations, contacts, security policies.
Passive reconActive recon
HowIndirectly, from public sources. You never touch the targetDirectly talking to the target's systems
DetailLessMore
Risk of being noticedNoneYes
Toolsarchive.org, Whois, Netcraft, theHarvester, search enginesNMAP, Nessus, Metasploit, DNS/email enumeration

Passive tools

  • archive.org (Wayback Machine): old snapshots of a website, and when it changed. You can even download (mirror) a whole site to study its folders.
  • Whois: the public register for domain names. It shows the owner, contact details, IP address, name servers and registration/expiry dates.
  • Netcraft: finds a site's subdomains and what operating system its server runs.
  • Search operators (Google hacking):
OperatorFinds
site:example.comResults only from that site
inurl:loginPages with that word in the address
intitle:adminPages with that word in the title
filetype:pdfOnly that file type
cache:The search engine's stored copy of a page
"exact phrase"That exact wording
@wordSocial media results

Other passive sources: social media, forums, blogs, news alerts, and simply browsing the company website.

Active tools

  • DNS and mail server enumeration: query the target's DNS servers to list their records. This can reveal computer names, IP addresses and usernames, and hint at how big the organisation is. Tools: nslookup, host, dig.
  • Scanning: find live hosts, open ports, running services and versions, the operating system, and vulnerabilities. Tools: NMAP (and Zenmap, its GUI), Nessus, Nexpose.

NMAP basics

NMAP (Network Mapper) is a free, open-source scanner. The general form is:

nmap [scan type] [options] <target>

Its four main jobs:

  1. Host discovery: which computers are alive?
  2. Port scanning: which ports are open?
  3. Version detection: what service, and which version, is behind each port?
  4. OS detection: which operating system is it?

Host discovery ("ping sweeps")

TechniqueNMAP optionHow it worksNotes
ICMP echo sweep-PESend ICMP type 8 (Echo Request). A type 0 (Echo Reply) means alive; silence means down or filteredSimple, slow, easily blocked
Broadcast ICMPOne echo request to the broadcast address; every host repliesFaster, but most routers block it and Windows ignores it
Non-echo ICMP-PP (timestamp, type 13), -PM (address mask, type 17)Uses other ICMP questions that hosts still answerGets past filters that only block echo
TCP sweep-PS (SYN), -PA (ACK)Send a TCP packet to a common port (21, 22, 23, 25, 80)Also finds open ports; pick ports the firewall allows
UDP sweep-PUSend UDP. A "port unreachable" reply means that port is closed (but the host is up); silence is unclearNot very reliable; firewalls often drop UDP

Port scanning

ScanOptionWhat it sendsOpen portClosed portNotes
TCP Connect-sTThe full handshake: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACKHandshake completesRST/ACKReliable but noisy; shows up in the target's logs
TCP SYN ("half-open")-sSSYN only, then RST once it gets a SYN/ACKSYN/ACKRST/ACKNever completes the connection, so it's quieter
Stealth / inverse-sF (FIN), -sN (NULL), -sX (Xmas)Odd packets: FIN only, no flags, or FIN+URG+PSH all setNo replyRSTBy the TCP rules, closed ports must answer with RST and open ports ignore the packet. Slow, hard to detect
FTP bounce-bAsks an FTP server to connect to the target for youHides where you are; very slow

The key trick to remember: a SYN/ACK means open, and RST means closed. In stealth scans it's reversed: silence means open.

Version and OS detection

Different operating systems answer odd packets in slightly different ways. These differences are a TCP/IP fingerprint. For example:

  • Windows acknowledges certain packets with sequence number + 1; most others use the same number.
  • Linux sets a different Type-of-Service value in some error replies.

Options:

  • -O: OS detection (--osscan-guess to guess harder).
  • -sV: service version detection (--version-intensity 0–9).
  • -A: OS detection, versions, scripts and traceroute all together.

NMAP options cheat sheet

OptionMeaning
-sLJust list the targets; send nothing
-sP / -snPing scan: only check which hosts are up
-PnSkip discovery; treat every host as up
-p 22,80 / -p 1-65535Scan only these ports
-FFast: fewer ports (the top 100)
--top-ports NThe N most common ports
-rScan ports in order, not randomly
-sUUDP port scan
-sA / -sW / -sMACK / Window / Maimon scans
-n / -RNever / always do DNS name lookups
--reasonExplain why each port got its state

Defending against recon

  • Don't publish sensitive information; search for it yourself and remove what you find.
  • Use split DNS and block DNS zone transfers.
  • Turn off directory listing on web servers.
  • Train staff about social engineering.
  • Encrypt passwords and keep systems patched.
  • Hide server details ("server masking", disguised file extensions).
  • Watch logs for odd packets and half-finished connections.

🎯 What Assignment 4 tests

  • What a hypervisor does; what Whois can and can't tell you.
  • ICMP type 8 vs type 0; which -P options use TCP (-PS, -PA).
  • The handshake order; SYN-scan replies (SYN-ACK = open, RST = closed).
  • VirtualBox NAT behaviour.
  • -O / -sV / -A; ports 80 and 443 mean a website; the --reason output.

topics.title: Vulnerability scanning, system hacking and malware
topics.intro: Lectures 21–25. Week 4 found what's running on a system. This week is about finding its weaknesses, the kinds of attack that follow, and how each one is defended against. These notes cover the ideas and terms the exam asks about.
topics.html:
Vulnerability scanning

A vulnerability scan automatically checks a system for known weaknesses, such as out-of-date software or bad settings. Organisations run these on their own systems so they can fix problems before attackers find them.

ToolWhat to know
NMAP scripts (NSE)NMAP's add-on scripts. -sC (the same as --script=default) runs the default set, and -A includes them too
NessusThe best-known professional scanner. Easy to use, detailed reports, paid (7-day trial)
Nexpose, OpenVAS, MBSAOther vulnerability scanners

Script names describe their job: os-discovery identifies the operating system, enum-users lists accounts, and brute tries passwords.

Proxies

A proxy server sits in the middle and passes traffic on, so the other side sees the proxy's address instead of the real sender's. The course mentions this because attackers use proxies (and IP spoofing) to hide where an attack comes from. That's also why investigators can't always trust the source address in their logs.

System hacking

System hacking means breaking into a computer to steal or misuse what's on it. The course splits it into three stages.

a) Password attacks

Most of these succeed only because people choose weak or common passwords.

MethodIdea
Shoulder surfingWatching someone type
Social engineeringTricking a person into revealing it
Dictionary attackTrying a list of common words
Brute forceTrying every possible combination
Rule-basedTrying variations when part of the password is known
Default passwordsDevices still using the factory password
Keyloggers / spywareHidden software recording what you type
Wire sniffingCapturing passwords sent unencrypted over the network
Rainbow tablesPre-computed lists of passwords and their hashes

Tools named in the course: John the Ripper, Hydra, Hashcat, Crunch (Crunch only makes wordlists).

Why length matters: each extra character multiplies the number of guesses. Four lowercase letters give 26⁴ = 456,976 combinations; eight give about 209 billion.

Defences: long passphrases, no reused or default passwords, locking accounts after failed attempts, and two-factor login.

b) Privilege escalation

After getting in with an ordinary account, the attacker tries to gain more power, using bugs or misconfigurations.

  • Vertical: going up a level, e.g. normal user → administrator.
  • Horizontal: staying at the same level but taking over another user's account.

Defences: give every program and user the least privilege they need, limit who can log in interactively, encrypt sensitive data, and keep software patched.

c) Running programs and hiding files

With access, attackers may run programs remotely, take screenshots, or install a backdoor so they can return. Legitimate remote-admin tools (the course names PDQ Deploy and DameWare) can be misused for this.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) damages systems or gives control to its creator.

TypeWhat it does
VirusCopies itself by attaching to other files or programs; spreads when they're shared
WormCopies itself across networks on its own, no host file needed
TrojanPretends to be useful software; does not copy itself. Often opens a backdoor
RansomwareLocks your files and demands payment
Spyware / adwareSpies on you / shows unwanted ads
RootkitHides deep in the system to stay invisible
BotnetMany infected machines controlled together, often used for DDoS

A virus has an infection phase (copying itself) and an attack phase (doing damage when a trigger condition is met). Virus types named in the course: hoax, stealth, polymorphic (changes its own code to avoid detection).

How malware gets in: email attachments, USB drives, fake or pirated software, untrusted downloads, chat apps, and software bugs.

Signs of a Trojan: antivirus mysteriously switched off, browser redirects, strange network activity.

Defences: genuine antivirus, firewalls, timely updates, no unknown attachments or sites, strong passwords.

Antivirus is tested safely with the EICAR test file: a harmless string that all antivirus products agree to flag.

Attacks on the local network

Packet sniffing means capturing the traffic on a network, like tapping a phone line. A network card in promiscuous mode keeps every packet it sees, not just its own.

  • Passive sniffing: on old networks with hubs, everyone sees all traffic, so just listening is enough.
  • Active sniffing: modern switches only send traffic where it belongs, so attackers try to trick the switch (below).

Protocols that send passwords in plain text (readable by a sniffer): HTTP, Telnet, rlogin, FTP, POP, IMAP, SMTP. Their encrypted versions (HTTPS, SSH, etc.) protect against this.

AttackIdeaResult
MAC floodingFill the switch's CAM table (its list of which device is on which port) with fake entriesThe switch falls back to sending traffic to every port, like a hub
DHCP starvationRequest every available IP address with fake requestsReal devices can't get an address (a DoS)
ARP spoofing / poisoningSend fake ARP replies so devices link the attacker's MAC to someone else's IPTraffic flows through the attacker: man-in-the-middle

Defences: switch port security (limiting MAC addresses per port), DHCP snooping, static or inspected ARP entries, and encrypting traffic so captured data is unreadable.

🎯 What Assignment 5 tests

  • Which NMAP options run scripts (-A, -sC, --script=default).
  • Which tools are not scanners (Hydra, Crunch).
  • Packet sniffing is not a password-cracking method.
  • UDP is connectionless; Crunch makes wordlists.
  • Not all malware self-replicates (Trojans don't).
  • MAC flooding makes a switch act like a hub.
  • smb-os-discovery.
  • Counting maths: usernames × passwords = 4 × 5000 = 20,000; 26⁴ = 456,976.

topics.title: Cryptography: private and public key
topics.intro: Lectures 26–30. This is the start of the cryptography weeks: how to keep data secret and prove who sent it. You don't need to do hard maths, only understand the ideas and remember a few numbers.
topics.html:
Types of security attack

Picture a message going from a Source (S) to a Destination (D), with an Intruder (I) nearby.

AttackWhat the intruder doesSecurity goal it breaks
InterruptionBlocks or destroys the messageAvailability
InterceptionSecretly reads itConfidentiality
ModificationChanges it on the wayIntegrity
FabricationCreates a fake messageAuthenticity

Passive vs active attacks

  • Passive: only listening, never changing anything. Examples: reading message contents, or traffic analysis (studying who talks to whom and how often). These are very hard to detect.
  • Active: changing data or creating false data. Four types:
    • Masquerade: pretending to be someone else.
    • Replay: recording a real message and resending it later.
    • Modification: altering part of a message.
    • Denial of service: blocking access.

Security services (what we want to provide)

ServicePlain meaning
ConfidentialityPrivacy: only the intended people can read it
AuthenticationProof of who created or sent it
IntegrityProof it wasn't changed
Non-repudiationThe sender can't later deny sending it
Access controlOnly allowed people can use a resource
AvailabilityIt works when needed

Encryption basics

  • Plaintext (P): the readable message.
  • Ciphertext (C): the scrambled version.
  • Key (K): the secret value that controls the scrambling.

A golden rule: a cipher's security should depend only on keeping the key secret, never on hiding how the algorithm works. Assume everyone knows the algorithm.

Private-key (symmetric)Public-key (asymmetric)
KeysOne shared secret keyA pair per person: public + private
SpeedFast (DES is about 100× faster than RSA)Slow
Big problemSharing the key safely; needs n(n−1)/2 keys for n peopleSlow; needs a way to trust public keys
ExamplesCaesar, DES, 3DES, IDEA, AESRSA, Diffie-Hellman

Classical ciphers (pen-and-paper)

Substitution: swap letters for other letters

  • Caesar cipher: shift every letter 3 places forward, wrapping Z → A. HAPPY NEW YEAR → KDSSB QHZ BHDU.
    • The general version shifts by k places, and k is the key.
    • Weakness: only 25 possible keys, so just try them all (brute force).
  • Mono-alphabetic cipher: any letter can map to any other letter, following a fixed table (the key).
    • There are 26! (about 4 × 10²⁶) possible keys.
    • Still weak: some letters are much more common than others (like E in English), so letter-frequency analysis breaks it.

Transposition: keep the letters, change their order

One simple method: write the message in rows under numbered columns, then read the columns out in key order.

Weakness: the ciphertext has exactly the same letter counts as the original.

Stream vs block ciphers

  • Stream: encrypts bit by bit.
  • Block: encrypts fixed-size chunks (e.g. 64 or 128 bits), padding the last chunk if it's short.

Modern private-key ciphers

CipherBlock sizeKey sizeNotes
DES64 bits56 bitsOld US standard. 16 rounds (a "Feistel" structure). The key is now too short
Triple DES64 bitsUp to 168 bitsRuns DES three times: Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt with 3 keys. Secure but slow
IDEA64 bits128 bits
AES (Rijndael)128 bits128, 192 or 256 bitsToday's standard (chosen in 2000). 10, 12 or 14 rounds

Each AES round has four steps: SubBytes (substitute), ShiftRows (shuffle), MixColumns (mix), AddRoundKey (add the key).

Public-key cryptography

Each person has two keys:

  • A public key, shared with everyone, like an open padlock.
  • A private key, kept secret, the only key that opens that padlock.

What is locked with one key can only be opened with the other.

GoalSender A usesReceiver B usesWhy
Confidentiality (secret message to B)B's public keyB's private keyOnly B can open it
Authentication (proving it came from A)A's private keyA's public keyOnly A could have made it

Three uses: encryption, digital signatures, and key exchange.

RSA

Invented by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977. It's safe because splitting a huge number into its two prime factors is extremely hard. Safe key sizes are around 1024–2048 bits.

Key generation:

  1. Pick two primes p and q, and compute n = p × q.
  2. Compute φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).
  3. Pick e that shares no factor with φ(n).
  4. Find d so that (d × e) leaves remainder 1 when divided by φ(n).
  5. The public key is {e, n}; the private key is {d, n}.

Encrypt: C = M^e mod n. Decrypt: M = C^d mod n.

Worked example (from the slides):

  • p = 7, q = 17 → n = 119, φ(n) = 96.
  • Choose e = 5. Then d = 77, because 77 × 5 = 385 = 4 × 96 + 1.
  • Public key {5, 119}, private key {77, 119}.
  • Encrypt M = 19: 19⁵ mod 119 = 66. Decrypt: 66⁷⁷ mod 119 = 19.

In practice: RSA is slow, so it's used only to send a random AES key safely, and AES then encrypts the actual data. Quantum computers could break RSA in future, which is why "post-quantum" algorithms are being researched.

Diffie-Hellman key exchange (1976)

Lets two people agree on a shared secret key over a public channel, without ever sending the key itself. It can't encrypt messages on its own; it only creates a key.

  1. A and B publicly agree on two numbers, n and g.
  2. A picks a secret x and sends X = g^x mod n.
  3. B picks a secret y and sends Y = g^y mod n.
  4. Both work out the same key, gxy mod n. A computes Y^x; B computes X^y.

It's safe because working backwards from X to x (the "discrete logarithm") is very hard. Weakness: a man-in-the-middle can sit between them, do the exchange separately with each, and read everything.

Message authentication

How do you prove a message wasn't changed and came from the right person?

  • Encrypt it with a key only the two of you share.
  • Attach a MAC (Message Authentication Code), computed from the message and a secret key: MAC = F(K, M).
    • The receiver recomputes it. If it matches, the message is genuine and unchanged.
  • Hash functions (covered in Week 7):
FamilyOutput size
MD5 (also MD2, MD4)128 bits
SHA-1160 bits
SHA-256 / 384 / 512256 / 384 / 512 bits
RIPEMD-128 / 160128 / 160 bits

🎯 What Assignment 6 tests

  • Masquerade vs replay vs modification.
  • Caesar shift encrypt and decrypt (SECURE → VHFXUH, KHOOR → HELLO).
  • Using a substitution table (CODE → EGRT).
  • Hashes can't be reversed; DoS = interruption.
  • Encrypt with the receiver's public key; DES block = 64 bits.
  • Key counting: public-key = 2N keys (150 people → 300); symmetric = N(N−1)/2 (40 people → 780).

topics.title: Hashes, digital signatures and secure protocols
topics.intro: Lectures 31–35. Week 6 showed how to keep data secret. This week covers how to prove data wasn't changed (hashes), prove who sent it (signatures and certificates), and the real protocols that use all of this (SSL/TLS, SSH, IPSec).
topics.html:
Hash functions

A hash function turns a message of any size into a short, fixed-size "fingerprint" called the digest.

  • One-way: you can't get the message back from the hash.
  • Many-to-one: infinitely many messages map onto a limited number of hashes, so matching pairs ("collisions") must exist. They should just be impossible to find.

What a good cryptographic hash must do:

  1. Work on input of any size.
  2. Always give the same, fixed-length output.
  3. Be quick to compute.
  4. First preimage resistance: given a hash, you can't find a message that produces it.
  5. Second preimage resistance: given one message, you can't find a different message with the same hash.
  6. Collision resistance: you can't find any two messages with the same hash. This is the strongest requirement.

Avalanche effect: change one letter of the message and the whole hash changes completely.

Keyed vs unkeyed hashes

Unkeyed hash (MDC)Keyed hash (MAC)
InputMessage onlyMessage + secret key
ProvesIntegrity (not changed), if you got the hash from a trusted sourceIntegrity and who sent it (authenticity)
WeaknessAnyone can recompute it after changing the messageThe key must be shared
ExamplesMD5, SHA-256HMAC

Hash families and sizes

HashOutput (digest)Block sizeRounds
MD5128 bits512 bits
SHA-1160 bits512 bits80
SHA-224 / SHA-256224 / 256 bits512 bits64
SHA-384 / SHA-512384 / 512 bits1024 bits80
RIPEMD-128 / 160128 / 160 bits

HMAC: a keyed hash built from an ordinary hash

HMAC hashes twice, mixing in the key each time:

HMAC(M) = H(K ‖ P ‖ H(K ‖ Q ‖ M))

Here K is the key, P and Q are fixed padding values, and ‖ means "join together". Hashing is faster than encryption, and hash code is available everywhere, which is why HMAC is popular.

The birthday attack

It's like the birthday puzzle: in a room of only 23 people, two probably share a birthday. For an n-bit hash, trying about 2n/2 random messages will probably turn up a collision. So hashes need at least 128 bits, and 160 or more is recommended.

Digital signatures

A digital signature is the electronic version of a handwritten signature, built on public-key cryptography.

  • Sign with your private key. Only you have it, so nobody else can forge your signature.
  • Verify with your public key. Anyone can check it, and you don't need to be online.

This gives authentication (who signed), integrity (nothing changed) and non-repudiation (the signer can't deny it).

Usual method (signature with appendix): hash the message, sign the hash, and send the message plus the signature. The receiver hashes the message themselves and checks it matches the signature.

Other kinds of signature:

  • With message recovery: the message itself comes back out of the signature.
  • Deterministic: same message, same signature every time.
  • Probabilistic: a different signature each time; harder to forge.
  • Blind: the signer signs without seeing the message (used for e.g. anonymous voting).
  • Undeniable: the signer must take part in verifying it.

Examples: RSA, DSA, ECDSA, ElGamal, Schnorr.

Attacks on signatures, from worst to least bad:

  • Total break: the attacker has the signing key.
  • Selective forgery: the attacker can sign messages of their choice.
  • Existential forgery: the attacker can sign some messages, but can't control which.

Digital certificates

The problem: how do you know a public key really belongs to, say, your bank? The answer: a certificate.

A digital certificate links a public key to an identity (a name and details). It is signed by a trusted Certification Authority (CA).

  • The common format is X.509 v3. It holds a version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity dates, subject name, subject's public key, and optional fields.
  • A certificate can be revoked if it expires or its private key is compromised. The CA publishes a Certificate Revocation List (CRL).

SSL/TLS: securing web traffic

SSL (Secure Socket Layer) was created by Netscape. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is its successor. Both sit between the application (HTTP, email) and TCP.

Goals: authenticate the server (and optionally the client), keep data private, and keep it unchanged.

SSL has two layers:

  • Record protocol: splits data into chunks of 16 KB or less, compresses them, adds a MAC, encrypts, and hands the result to TCP.
  • Three protocols on top of it:
    • Handshake: agree on algorithms and keys, and authenticate.
    • ChangeCipherSpec: "switch to the agreed settings now".
    • Alert: warnings or fatal errors (a fatal alert ends the session).

The handshake in four phases:

  1. Hello: client and server exchange version, a random number, session ID and the list of ciphers they support.
  2. Server: sends its certificate and key exchange information, and may request the client's certificate.
  3. Client: sends its certificate (if asked) and key exchange information.
  4. Finish: both send ChangeCipherSpec and Finished. From here on, data is encrypted.

Secure versions of services:

ServicePort
HTTPS443
SMTP over SSL465
POP3 over SSL995
LDAP over SSL636 (the slide says 646)

Note that SSL/TLS adds work, so it is not faster than plain HTTP, and it does not provide non-repudiation.

SSH (Secure Shell)

Created in 1995 as a secure replacement for Telnet, rlogin and rcp. It encrypts everything, including passwords, and supports tunnelling (port forwarding).

In SSH version 1, the server has two keys:

  • A long-term identity key (1024-bit RSA).
  • A short-term encryption key (768-bit RSA), replaced every hour so old sessions can't be decrypted later.

Login can use a password, RSA keys, or plug-ins (smart cards, biometrics).

IPSec: security at the IP layer

IPSec adds encryption and authentication to IP itself. It is required in IPv6 and optional in IPv4.

It provides authentication and integrity, confidentiality, and replay protection (re-sent copies of packets are dropped).

ModeProtectsUsed between
TransportOnly the payload; the original IP header stays visibleTwo hosts
TunnelThe entire original packet, wrapped inside a new oneFirewalls or hosts; this is how VPNs work

Its downsides: it's complex, doesn't work well with NAT, and routers must support it.

S-HTTP vs HTTPS

  • HTTPS = HTTP running over SSL/TLS. It secures the whole connection.
  • S-HTTP = an extension of HTTP that secures individual messages. It can work with symmetric keys only.

They are not the same thing, and HTTPS is the one used today.

🎯 What Assignment 7 tests

  • Hash output is fixed-length and smaller than the message.
  • DES block 64 bits; MD5 = 128 bits; SHA-256 = 256-bit output; SHA-512 block = 1024 bits.
  • HTTPS relies on SSL/TLS; collision resistance (no two messages with the same hash).
  • Verify a signature with the signer's public key; non-repudiation.
  • Unkeyed hashes don't prove authenticity.
  • IPSec transport mode keeps the original IP header.

topics.title: Steganography, biometrics and network attacks
topics.intro: Lectures 36–40. Five topics this week: hiding data inside files, identifying people by their bodies, attacks that knock services offline, and keeping DNS and email trustworthy. The attack sections explain how each one works and how it's stopped. That is the level the exam asks about.
topics.html:
Steganography: hiding that a message exists

Steganography is Greek for "covered writing": hiding a message inside something innocent-looking.

EncryptionSteganography
GoalMake the message unreadableMake the message invisible
Draws attention?Yes; scrambled text looks suspiciousNo; it looks like a normal photo

The two can be combined: encrypt the message first, then hide it.

Digital watermarking uses the same techniques, but to embed copyright or ownership information rather than a secret.

Historical examples:

  • A message tattooed on a messenger's shaved head, with the hair allowed to grow back.
  • A WWII spy letter where the second letter of each word spelled the real message.

The formula: cover medium + hidden message + stego key = stego medium.

Good covers: images, audio, video, program files, text.

Hiding data in images

Every pixel is a colour made of Red, Green and Blue, each 0–255 (one byte). For example, FF 00 00 = red and FF FF FF = white.

  • GIF: 8 bits per pixel, at most 256 colours (each pixel points into a colour table). Lossless compression.
  • JPEG: 24 bits per pixel. Lossy compression, based on the DCT (discrete cosine transform).
  • BMP: 24 bits per pixel.

The main method: LSB (Least Significant Bit) insertion. Change only the last bit of each pixel's value. That shifts the colour so slightly nobody can see it.

  • 1 bit hidden per pixel.
  • 8 pixels hide 1 character (8 bits).
  • Simple, works best with 24-bit and grayscale images.
  • Easily destroyed if the image is edited or recompressed.

Example: to hide "C" (ASCII 67 = 01000011), set the last bit of 8 pixels to 0,1,0,0,0,0,1,1.

Capacity maths: bytes hidden = number of pixels ÷ 8. A 1500 × 1200 image = 1,800,000 pixels = 225,000 bytes.

Other methods:

  • Masking and filtering: subtly brighten certain areas, usually busy or noisy parts of the picture.
  • Algorithms and transformations: hide data inside the maths of JPEG's DCT compression. The most sophisticated approach.

Biometrics: identifying people by their bodies

Biometrics means recognising a person automatically from measurable features of their body or behaviour.

Physical (what you are)Behavioural (how you act)
Fingerprint, face, hand geometry, iris, retina, DNASignature dynamics (speed, pressure), keystroke rhythm, gait (walk), voice
BiometricNotes from the course
FingerprintMatches ridge details ("minutiae"); sometimes unreliable
Hand geometryMore accurate than fingerprints, but needs a larger scanner
IrisInfrared scan of the eye's coloured ring; very distinctive
RetinaAmong the most secure, unique even to each eye; uncomfortable for the user
FaceAffected by lighting and background
VoicePitch, intensity, duration; background noise causes problems

Multimodal biometrics combines several features (e.g. face + voice), because no single one is accurate enough on its own.

Uses:

  • Commercial: logins, payments, building access.
  • Government: passports, border control, Aadhaar.
  • Forensic: criminal investigations, missing persons.

Denial of Service (DoS) attacks

A DoS attack tries to stop real users from reaching a service, usually by overwhelming it.

AttackHow it works (concept)Defence
SmurfPings are sent to a network's broadcast address with the victim's address faked as the sender, so every host on that network replies to the victim at onceRouters reject outside packets addressed to broadcast addresses
Ping of DeathAn oversized ping (over 65,535 bytes, the IP maximum) arrives in fragments. When reassembled it overflows the receiver, and older systems crashPatched systems simply discard oversized packets
SYN floodMany SYNs with faked source addresses. The server reserves space for each half-open connection until the table is fullSYN cookies (below)

Why SYN floods work: sending a SYN costs the attacker nothing, but the server spends memory on every one. The cost is lopsided.

SYN cookies, the fix: the server doesn't store anything when a SYN arrives. Instead it encodes the connection details in a cryptographic value (the "cookie") and puts it in its SYN-ACK. Only when a real client sends back the final ACK carrying that cookie does the server recreate the state and open the connection.

Distributed DoS (DDoS)

A DDoS attack comes from many machines at once, usually a botnet (infected computers controlled through "handler" machines). That makes it much harder to block, and the person behind it may not even be online during the attack.

HTTP flood: bots send huge numbers of normal-looking web requests.

  • GET flood: requests for pages, images and files.
  • POST flood: form submissions, which are expensive because each one makes the server do database work.
  • Defences: CAPTCHA or JavaScript challenges to tell bots from people, a web application firewall, and IP reputation lists.

General DoS/DDoS defences:

  • ISPs: anti-spoofing filters (very important), turn off directed broadcasts, monitor traffic volumes.
  • Servers: watch for unusual traffic, disable unused UDP services.
  • Everyone: install security patches, and scan regularly for malware so your machines don't become bots.

DNS security

DNS turns names (www.gmail.com) into IP addresses. It also supports aliases (several names for one host) and load balancing (several IPs for one name).

It's a hierarchy of servers:

  1. Root servers know where the ".com" servers are.
  2. The .com servers know where gmail.com's server is.
  3. gmail.com's own server gives the final IP address.
  • Iterative lookup: each server replies "ask this server next".
  • Recursive lookup: the server does all the asking for you and returns the answer.
  • Caching: servers remember answers for a while, so they don't ask the root every time.

Why DNS is weak: most queries travel in plain text over UDP (easy to fake), and responses aren't authenticated.

DNS cache poisoning: a fake answer gets accepted and stored in a DNS server's cache. Everyone who uses that server is then sent to the wrong website.

DNSSEC, the fix: DNS answers are digitally signed at every level, which guarantees where the answer came from and that it wasn't changed. The downside is bigger packets and more load on servers.

Email security: PGP

PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) secures email and stored files. It's popular because it's free, runs everywhere, uses well-known algorithms, and isn't controlled by any government.

Its five services:

  • Authentication: a digital signature proves the sender.
  • Confidentiality: encryption keeps the message private.
  • Compression: ZIP, applied after signing.
  • Email compatibility: base-64 encoding, so binary data survives email systems.
  • Segmentation: splits large messages into 50 KB pieces.

🎯 What Assignment 8 tests

  • Steganography = hiding inside a cover; valid examples (image, audio, executable).
  • Behavioural biometrics (signature, gait, keystrokes); the iris is the most reliable.
  • DoS definition; how Smurf and SYN flood work.
  • PGP = authentication + confidentiality; DNS = names to IP addresses.
  • LSB capacity: pixels ÷ 8 = bytes.

topics.title: Sniffing, social engineering and DoS
topics.intro: Lectures 41–45. This week covers three ways attackers get information or disrupt services without breaking any cryptography: listening to network traffic (sniffing), tricking people (social engineering), and overloading services (DoS). For each, the notes explain the idea, name the tools the course mentions, and list the defences.
topics.html:
Sniffing and network analysis

Sniffing (network analysis) means capturing the traffic travelling across a network and reading it. The same tools are used by network admins to fix problems and by attackers to spy.

Good analysers support many protocols, have a graphical interface, and produce statistics.

Wireshark

Wireshark is the best-known free analyser. It captures and displays traffic in readable form, keeps logs for investigations, and filters by protocol. It only watches: it can't change live traffic and isn't an attack tool.

Its screen has three parts:

  • Packet list: number, time, source, destination, protocol, length, info.
  • Packet details: each layer's header, broken down.
  • Raw bytes: the data in hex and ASCII.

Type a filter such as http or dns in the filter bar. It turns green when the filter is valid and red when it isn't.

How capture works:

  • The network card is switched to promiscuous mode (this needs admin/root rights), so it keeps every frame on its segment, not just frames addressed to it.
  • On a hub, that means everyone's traffic.
  • On a switch, you mostly see only your own traffic. That's why switches are safer than hubs.

Why unencrypted protocols are dangerous

With HTTP, FTP or Telnet, a sniffer can read usernames and passwords directly. With HTTPS, SSL/TLS or SSH, it only sees scrambled data.

Other tools named in the course

ToolWhat it is
EttercapA man-in-the-middle tool for LANs. IP/MAC filtering, injecting characters into live connections, filtering or dropping packets, plug-ins, OS fingerprinting. It does not do SQL injection or dictionary password cracking
Burp SuiteA web-application security testing platform (Java, by PortSwigger). Modules: Target, Proxy (sits between your browser and the server so you can inspect traffic), Spider (crawler), Scanner, Intruder, Repeater
SolarWinds, KismetOther network analysers

Defending against sniffing

  • Encrypt everything: HTTPS not HTTP, SSH not Telnet, SFTP/SCP not FTP, SSL/TLS for email, VPN/IPSec, PGP or S/MIME for messages.
  • Use switches, not hubs.
  • Restrict physical access to network sockets and cables.
  • Use static ARP entries (especially for the gateway) so fake ARP replies can't redirect traffic.
  • Use one-time passwords.
  • Detect sniffers: NMAP's sniffer-detect script checks whether a machine on the local network has its card in promiscuous mode.

Recap from Week 5: ARP spoofing. Fake ARP replies make victims send their traffic to the attacker's machine, turning a switched network into a man-in-the-middle situation.

Social engineering: hacking people

Social engineering means persuading or tricking people into giving away confidential information. It often works by appealing to greed ("something for nothing"), fear or helpfulness.

Common targets: help-desk staff, technical support, system administrators, unhappy employees.

The four phases:

  1. Research the company: websites, employees, even rubbish bins ("dumpster diving").
  2. Pick a victim: the most vulnerable person.
  3. Build a relationship with them.
  4. Exploit it to get the information.

The three types

TypeExamples
Human-based (in person or by voice)Impersonation (pretending to be IT staff or a manager, the most common); reverse social engineering (posing as an expert so the victim comes to you for help); piggybacking (an authorised person knowingly lets you through a door: "I forgot my badge"); tailgating (slipping in closely behind someone, perhaps with a fake badge); eavesdropping; shoulder surfing
Computer-basedPhishing (fake emails or sites pretending to be your bank, etc.); spear phishing (phishing aimed at one specific person or small group); fake pop-up windows; chain letters ("forward to 10 people for a prize"); chatting to collect personal details
Mobile-basedFake or malicious apps with names like popular ones; SMS messages pretending to be your bank and asking you to call a number

Quick rule: if it needs the attacker physically present or on the phone, it's human-based. If it arrives on a screen (email, pop-up, chain letter), it's computer-based.

The course demo uses the Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET) to show, in the lab, how convincing a fake login page can be.

Defences

  • Training: the most important defence. Policies are useless if staff don't know them.
  • Password policy: regular changes, no guessable passwords, lock accounts after failed attempts.
  • Physical security: ID cards, escorted visitors, restricted areas.
  • Least access: separate admin, user and guest accounts.
  • Classify information (top secret, internal, public, ...).
  • Background checks, and a proper process when people leave.
  • Layered anti-virus and anti-phishing at both the user and mail-server level.
  • Two-factor authentication for important services.

Denial of Service, revisited

A DoS attack reduces or blocks access to a service by flooding it with bogus requests. A DDoS uses many compromised machines (a botnet) at once.

CategoryIdea
Bandwidth attacksUse up the network's capacity; needs many machines
SYN floodHalf-open TCP connections fill the server's listen queue. Each one is held for about 75 seconds waiting for the final ACK, which never comes
ICMP floodHuge numbers of ICMP (ping) packets
Application-level floodTargets a specific application, e.g. repeated failed logins that lock out a real user

Tools the course names (you only need to recognise them):

  • Slowloris: opens many connections to a web server and sends each request incompletely and very slowly, so the server's connection slots stay tied up. It needs very little bandwidth.
  • LOIC (Low Orbit Ion Cannon): a "stress-testing" tool that floods a target with TCP, UDP or HTTP traffic.
  • R.U.D.Y. ("R U Dead Yet?"): a "low and slow" attack that submits web forms one tiny piece at a time.

Defences:

  • Keep anti-virus and anti-Trojan software up to date, so your machines don't become bots.
  • Disable unnecessary services and uninstall unused applications.
  • Scan files from outside sources.
  • Add bandwidth on critical links, and replicate servers for backup.
  • Raise security awareness.
  • As a last resort, shut services down until the attack passes.
  • Also see Week 8: SYN cookies, web application firewalls, anti-spoofing filters.

🎯 What Assignment 9 tests

  • Sniffing = capturing traffic; promiscuous mode.
  • Wireshark can't modify traffic or do SQL injection.
  • Plain-text protocols (HTTP, FTP, Telnet) can be sniffed.
  • What Ettercap can't do (SQL injection, dictionary attacks).
  • Phishing is computer-based, not human-based.
  • SYN flooding; Slowloris = partial HTTP requests.
  • Computer-based social engineering examples (phishing, pop-ups, chain letters).
  • ARP spoofing = traffic routed through the attacker.

topics.title: Hardware security
topics.intro: Lectures 46–50. So far, every attack has targeted software or networks. This week the target is the chip itself. The main lesson: an encryption algorithm can be mathematically perfect and still leak its secret key through the hardware running it.
topics.html:
Why hardware security matters

"Hardware" here means processors, memory and firmware, but also small security devices: SIM cards (they hold your subscriber identity), RFID tags (unique ID codes), smart cards (secret keys) and PUFs (section 4).

Three kinds of threat:

  • Physical attacks: done on the device itself, with lab equipment.
  • Planned attacks: a weakness deliberately built into the chip (a hardware Trojan, section 5).
  • Stealing secrets: reading the confidential data a device carries.

Types of hardware attack

AttackHow it worksInvasive?
Black-box testingFeed in inputs, watch the outputs, and work out the algorithmNo
Physical probingPlace tiny probes on the chip's wires and read data directlyYes
Reverse engineeringStrip the chip layer by layer and photograph each oneYes
Side-channel analysisMeasure timing, power or radio emissions during normal useNo

Invasive means the chip is physically opened or damaged. Only probing and reverse engineering are invasive.

Countermeasures

  • Scramble or encrypt the data inside the chip's registers and buses.
  • Disguise the layout: 3D stacking, dummy circuits.
  • Metal mesh over the circuit: probing it causes a short, which wipes the stored secrets.
  • Side-channel defences: random noise generators, hiding secrets (section 3).
  • PUFs, for low-cost security protocols.

Side-channel attacks

A side channel is anything a device leaks unintentionally while it works: how long it takes, how much power it draws, radio (electromagnetic) emissions, heat, faulty outputs, or test data.

The important point: side-channel attacks don't question the maths of the algorithm. They attack its implementation, so the attacker usually needs to be near the device, or have it in hand.

Timing attacks

Paul Kocher published the first one in 1995. If a calculation takes longer for some key bits than for others, then timing it many times can reveal the key.

Example: square-and-multiply. RSA and Diffie-Hellman compute big powers like x^e. To do this quickly, go through the bits of e:

  • Every bit needs a squaring.
  • A 1 bit also needs a multiplication.

So multiplications only happen on 1 bits, and the total time reveals how many 1s are in the key.

FormulaMeaning
Time = n × t_square + k × t_multiplyn = number of key bits, k = number of 1 bits. Time leaks k
Fixed: Time = n × (t_square + t_multiply)Do a dummy multiplication on 0 bits too, so the time no longer depends on the key

Counting operations (assignment style): for x²², write 22 in binary: 10110 (5 bits, three 1s).

  • Squarings = bits − 1 = 4.
  • Multiplications = number of 1s − 1 = 2.
  • Slide example: x¹³ = 1101 gives 3 squarings and 2 multiplications, instead of 12 multiplications done the slow way.

Power analysis attacks

These were introduced in 1998 and are more powerful than timing attacks. The attacker measures the device's power consumption while it encrypts. A recording of power over time is called a trace.

SPA (Simple Power Analysis)DPA (Differential Power Analysis)
Traces neededOne, or a fewMany
MethodLook at the trace and spot patterns, e.g. the rounds of AES, or a square vs a multiplySplit the traces into two groups by a guessed key bit, average each group, subtract. A peak means the guess was right
StrengthEasier to defend againstMore powerful: finds leaks too small to see in any single trace

Defences against side channels

  • Against timing: make the run time independent of the data. Use constant-time code, or add dummy operations so every path takes equally long. This is relatively easy.
  • Against power analysis (harder):
    • Hardware: special low-leakage logic styles, masking, noise generators, random interruptions to break up the timing.
    • Software: avoid predictable intermediate values, add redundant computations, and mask data by mixing in a secret random value.

Note that masking protects against power leaks, not timing leaks. Making code more complicated without fixing the timing differences does nothing.

A catch: a defence against one side channel can open up another. This is still an active research area.

PUFs: Physically Unclonable Functions

No two chips come out of the factory exactly alike; there are tiny random variations. A PUF turns those variations into a fingerprint for the chip.

It works by challenge and response: give it an n-bit input (the challenge), and it returns an n-bit output (the response) that depends on that particular chip's physical quirks.

Four properties to know:

PropertyMeaning
EvaluableWorking out the response for a challenge is quick and easy
UniqueThe response identifies that specific chip
UnclonableNobody, not even the manufacturer, can build another chip that gives the same responses
One-wayGiven a response, you can't work back to the challenge

Why PUFs are useful:

  • No stored key to steal. Normally a secret key sits in memory, where an attacker might extract it. With a PUF, the key is generated from the chip's own physics when needed, and deleted afterwards.
  • Anti-counterfeiting. Record each genuine chip's challenge-response pairs at the factory. Later, test any chip: a fake won't give matching answers.
  • Key generation. The PUF response seeds a public/private key pair created on the chip itself.

Kinds of PUF:

  • Arbiter PUF: two signals race along paths chosen by the challenge; whichever arrives first decides the bit.
  • Ring-oscillator PUF: compares the frequencies of two oscillators.
  • SRAM PUF: the random 0/1 values memory cells take when the power first comes on.
  • The course also shows a simple latch-based PUF built on an FPGA.

Hardware Trojans

A hardware Trojan is a malicious, deliberate change to a chip's circuitry, made during design or manufacturing.

  • It has a trigger (a condition that wakes it up, e.g. a rare input, or a counter reaching a value: a "time bomb").
  • And a payload (what it does then: malfunction, leak secret data, shut down).

Why they're a real worry: modern chips are built from third-party design blocks with outside software tools, and are often made in overseas factories. Many parties touch the design, and not all of them are trusted.

Types:

  • Combinational: triggered by a rare combination of inputs.
  • Sequential: triggered by a sequence over time; counters act like time bombs.
  • Analog Trojans.
  • Information-leakage Trojans, including ones that leak through side channels.

Why they're hard to detect:

  • They add tiny amounts of extra circuitry: a few gates among billions.
  • Their triggers are rare by design.
  • There are endless possible kinds.
  • No single detection method catches them all, and every detection method adds its own cost in design, testing or run time.

Detection approaches: destructive (reverse engineering) or non-destructive (logic testing, side-channel measurements); at test time or while running.

A twist: Trojan-like techniques can be used for good too, e.g. to detect tampering or to fingerprint chips for copyright protection.

🎯 What Assignment 10 tests

  • Hardware attacks: probing, electromagnetic analysis.
  • Side channels attack the implementation, using timing, power or EM.
  • Square-and-multiply counting for x²² (4 squarings, 2 multiplications).
  • DPA needs many traces plus statistics; SPA reads one trace.
  • PUF evaluability; PUF = Physically Unclonable Function.
  • Hardware Trojan definition; Trojans are small and hard to detect.
  • Probing is invasive.
  • Timing defences: dummy operations and constant-time code (not masking).

topics.title: Web application attacks
topics.intro:
Lectures 51–55. This week moves to attacking websites and the databases behind them: the Metasploit framework, SQL injection, the sqlmap tool, and cross-site scripting. The notes stay at the level of ideas, terms and defences, which is what the exam asks about.

Why web servers are a favourite target: firewalls and good network settings now block most network- and OS-level attacks, but a web server has to be reachable from anywhere on the internet. That makes the application running on it the easiest way in.
topics.html:
The Metasploit framework

Metasploit is a penetration-testing platform: a big toolbox for finding a weakness and then taking advantage of it, all in one place. It comes with Kali Linux, is written in Ruby, and has a free and a paid version.

You drive it from the msfconsole (its command console). A separate tool, msfvenom, builds payloads.

The modules

ModuleWhat it is
ExploitThe code that takes advantage of a specific weakness. Over 2000 are included
PayloadWhat runs on the target after the exploit works, to set up a channel back to the attacker. Over 500
AuxiliaryHelpers that scan, brute-force or probe, but don't give control of the target
EncoderDisguises a payload so antivirus doesn't recognise its "bad" byte patterns
NOPSPadding that keeps a payload from crashing
PostFor deeper work after access is gained

Payloads worth knowing:

  • Command shell: run commands on the target.
  • Meterpreter: a powerful remote-control shell. It can browse, upload and download files, take screenshots, dump passwords, and try to become admin.

The commands

In Metasploit, show and search list things, and set chooses a value.

CommandDoes
searchFind an exploit or payload
use <name>Select a module
infoShow details of a module (which OS it hits, what to configure)
show targetsList the operating systems an exploit works against
set RHOSTSet the remote (target) IP; LHOST is your own machine
set RPORT / LPORTSet port numbers

The usual workflow: scan for a weakness → pick an exploit → configure it (target IP, port) → pick a payload → encode it → run the exploit.

Meterpreter commands: hashdump copies out password hashes (to crack offline with Hashcat), getuid shows who you are, getsystem tries for admin, sysinfo shows system details, ps lists running programs.

SQL injection

Many websites build a database question (a query) by pasting your input straight into it. SQL injection abuses that: you type database commands into an ordinary box (like a login field), and the site runs them.

It isn't a bug in any one program. It's the result of not checking user input, so the fix is always on the website's side.

Example (login bypass): the site runs

SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'INPUT1' AND password = 'INPUT2'

Type admin' OR '1'='1 as the username. The ' closes the username early, and OR '1'='1' is always true, so the check passes. Adding -- comments out the rest (the password check), so it's skipped.

Impact: data theft, altered or deleted data, denial of service, reputation damage.

Types of SQL injection:

TypeHow it tells the attacker what it found
Error-basedBad input makes the site show a raw database error, and the error leaks details of the query and tables
UNION-basedGlues an extra query onto the real one to pull out data
Blind – booleanThe site shows no errors, so the attacker asks true/false questions and reads the answer from how the page changes
Blind – time-basedReads the answer from how long the page takes to respond

Defence: validate and sanitise all input; never paste user input directly into a query (use parameterised queries); show generic error messages.

sqlmap

sqlmap is a free tool that automates SQL injection: it finds the flaw and then extracts the data for you. It supports MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite and more.

It can list databases, tables and columns, pull out users and password hashes, and even escalate privileges through Metasploit's Meterpreter.

Key options (they go from big to small):

OptionDoes
--dbsList all databases
--tablesList tables in a database
--columns (-C)List columns
--dumpCopy out the actual data
--current-dbThe database in use now
--current-userThe current user
--is-dbaIs the user a database admin?
--users / --passwordsList users / their password hashes
-D / -T / -CPick a database / table / column

Other web tools named this week: Dirb (brute-forces hidden folders and pages), Hydra, Acunetix.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

XSS sneaks the attacker's JavaScript into a web page so it runs in other visitors' browsers. The browser trusts the page, so the script can steal cookies and session tokens, or rewrite the page. Like SQL injection, it happens when a site uses user input in its output without checking it.

The three types:

TypeWhere the script livesExample
Stored (persistent, Type I)Saved on the server, e.g. in a comment or forum postEveryone who views that page is hit, including an admin reading feedback
Reflected (non-persistent, Type II)In a crafted link; the page bounces it straight backThe victim clicks a malicious link and the script runs
DOM-based (Type 0)Entirely in the browser: the page's own JavaScript puts the input into the page unsafelyThe data never even reaches the server

(The slides also mention "Server XSS" vs "Client XSS" as a newer way to group these.)

Defences: validate and encode user input, keep server software patched, block unsigned applets, and use content-filtering proxies.

File upload vulnerability

(Lecture 55 also covers this, with command injection.) If a site lets you upload a file but doesn't check what it is, you can upload a malicious script instead of, say, a photo, then run it on the server. Defence: check the file type and contents, rename uploads, and store them where they can't be executed.

🎯 What Assignment 11 tests

  • Metasploit modules: exploit vs payload vs encoder vs auxiliary.
  • msfconsole; show targets; set RHOST; hashdump.
  • Dirb brute-forces directories.
  • Error-based SQL injection shows a database error.
  • sqlmap --dbs lists databases.
  • The three real XSS types (stored, reflected, DOM).
  • Classic injection payloads (admin' OR '1'='1, ' OR 1=1 --).

topics.title: NMAP revisited, Wireshark and summary
topics.intro: Lectures 56–60. The final week is mostly revision: a deeper, more organised look at NMAP (first met in Weeks 4–5) and Wireshark (Week 9), then a wrap-up. Nothing is really new, so this is a good place to consolidate. The cheat sheet on the Overview tab pulls all the NMAP options together.
topics.html:
NMAP: the full picture
