NMAP (Network Mapper) is a free port scanner written by Gordon Lyon in 1997. One line sums up its job: it sends packets to a target and learns a lot from what comes back. Its four tasks, in order:

  1. Host discovery: which machines are alive?
  2. Port scanning: which ports are open?
  3. Service/version detection: what's running, and which version?
  4. OS detection: which operating system?

Host discovery (ping sweeps)

TechniqueOptionHow it works
ICMP echo-PEPing (type 8); a reply (type 0) means alive. Simple, slow, easily blocked
Broadcast ICMPOne ping to the broadcast address; everyone replies. Routers usually block it
Non-echo ICMP-PP (timestamp, type 13), -PM (address mask, type 17)Other ICMP questions that get past echo filters
TCP sweep-PS (SYN), -PA (ACK)TCP to a common port (21, 22, 23, 25, 80). Also shows open ports
UDP sweep-PUA "port unreachable" reply means closed. Unreliable

Port scans

ScanOptionOpen portClosed port
TCP Connect (full handshake)-sTHandshake completesRST/ACK
TCP SYN (half-open)-sSSYN/ACKRST/ACK
Stealth (FIN/NULL/Xmas)-sF / -sN / -sXNo replyRST
FTP bounce-b
UDP-sU

Remember the reversal: in a SYN scan, SYN/ACK = open, RST = closed. In stealth scans, silence = open.

Useful options

OptionMeaning
-sLJust list the targets; send nothing
-sn / -sPOnly check which hosts are up (no port scan)
-PnSkip discovery; assume every host is up
-p 22,80 / -p 1-65535Scan these ports
-FFast: the top 100 ports
--top-ports NThe N most common ports
-rScan in order, not randomly
-O / -sV / -AOS / version / everything
--reasonExplain each port's state
--script vulnRun vulnerability-check scripts

Counting questions (the exam likes these)

  • nmap --top-ports 20 target scans exactly 20 ports.
  • nmap -sL 10.10.5.100-115 covers 16 addresses: 115 − 100 + 1. Don't forget the +1.
  • -sn statement: host discovery only, no port scan. -Pn: skips discovery, goes straight to scanning. Both are true; they're opposites.

Scanning many targets

nmap 144.16.192.70           # one host
nmap 144.16.192.100-150      # a range
nmap 144.16.192.0/24         # a whole subnet
nmap -iL list.txt            # targets from a file
nmap 144.16.192.0/24 --exclude 144.16.192.60-70

Detection and evasion

  • OS/version detection relies on TCP/IP fingerprinting: operating systems answer odd packets slightly differently. For example, Windows acknowledges a certain packet with sequence number + 1; Linux sets a distinctive Type-of-Service value.
  • Admins spot scans by: checking logs for odd packets, connections that never finished, and unusual port usage.
  • Scanners avoid detection by: randomising port order, scanning very slowly, spoofing the source address, or coordinating several scanners.

Wireshark recap

Wireshark is the free network analyser (sniffer). It captures traffic and shows it in readable form, logs it for investigations, and filters it, but only watches, it never changes traffic.

  • It puts the network card in promiscuous mode (needs root) to keep every frame on the segment. On a switch, you mostly see only your own traffic.
  • Start a capture by double-clicking a network adapter or using the Capture menu.
  • Three panes: packet list (number, time, source, destination, protocol, length, info), packet details (each header expanded), and raw bytes (hex and ASCII).
  • Type a filter like tcp, ip or http in the filter bar: it turns green when valid, red when not.

Course wrap-up

Looking back, the course built up in layers, each one needed for the next:

  1. Weeks 1–3 – Networking: how data moves (packets, TCP/IP, addresses, routing). You can't attack what you don't understand.
  2. Weeks 4–5 – Finding targets: reconnaissance, scanning with NMAP, then finding weaknesses, cracking passwords and recognising malware.
  3. Weeks 6–7 – Cryptography: the defensive core, keeping data secret (encryption) and trustworthy (hashes, signatures, TLS).
  4. Weeks 8–9 – More attacks: steganography, biometrics, denial of service, sniffing and social engineering.
  5. Week 10 – Hardware: attacks on the chip itself, where even perfect maths can leak.
  6. Weeks 11–12 – Web and tools: Metasploit, SQL injection, XSS, then a final deep dive on NMAP and Wireshark.

The one idea to carry away: ethical hacking is about understanding how systems work well enough to find their weak points, so they can be fixed, always with permission, and always within the law.

🎯 What Assignment 12 tests

Almost entirely NMAP:

  • ICMP type 0 reply = host alive.
  • -PS/-PA are the TCP sweeps.
  • -sn does ICMP + TCP sweeps, not UDP.
  • -Pn treats all hosts as online.
  • -F scans the top 100 ports (not 1000).
  • -sU is the UDP scan; TCP Connect (-sT) completes the full handshake.
  • Counting: --top-ports 20 = 20; -sL 10.10.5.100-115 = 16.

quizIntros.W1: Topics: what ethical hacking is, how networks send data, and the TCP/IP headers. 10 questions, 1 mark each.

quizIntros.W3: Topics: how routers decide where packets go, routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, BGP) and IPv6. 10 questions. Watch out: Q2, Q6 and Q8 ask which statements are false.

quizIntros.W5: Topics: NMAP scripts, vulnerability scanners, password cracking, malware and attacks on network switches. 10 questions.
quizIntros.W6: Topics: types of attack, simple ciphers, hashing, and private-key vs public-key cryptography. 10 questions. Two kinds of encryption to know: - Symmetric (private-key): both people share the same secret key, like a house key with a copy. Example: DES, AES. - Asymmetric (public-key): each person has a pair. The public key is like an open padlock anyone can use to lock a box for you; the private key is the only key that opens it. Example: RSA.

quiz.q: What is ethical hacking?
quiz.why: The word "ethical" is the key. An ethical hacker is hired by the owner and has permission, like a locksmith the homeowner pays to test their locks. Option (a) describes a criminal hacker.
options: Unauthorized intrusion into a system or network to commit malicious acts (privacy invasion, data theft)
Systematically attempting to penetrate a system/network on behalf of its owner to find threats and vulnerabilities

quiz.q: Which application(s) are used to secure a personal laptop/desktop?
quiz.why: An antivirus finds and removes harmful programs. A firewall is a security guard that decides which network traffic may come in or go out. A virus and malware are the threats, not the protection.

quiz.q: What does LAN stand for?
quiz.why: LAN = Local Area Network: the network inside one home, office or building.

quiz.q: Which device is used to connect two different networks?
quiz.why: A router joins different networks, like your home Wi-Fi and the internet. A switch and a hub connect devices within one network. A repeater just boosts a weak signal.

quiz.q: Which protocol is used to send emails?
quiz.why: SMTP = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. FTP moves files, HTTP loads web pages, and SNMP manages network devices.

quiz.q: Which Linux command(s) can be used to view network configuration?
quiz.why: ifconfig shows your network settings (IP address and so on) on Linux. ipconfig is the Windows version. ls lists files and cd changes folder.

quiz.q: How many layers are there in the OSI model?
quiz.why: The OSI model splits networking into 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. A memory trick: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

quiz.q: Which of the following is/are transport layer protocol(s)?
quiz.why: TCP and UDP both work at the transport layer (layer 4). IP is at the network layer (3) and Ethernet at the data link layer (2).

quiz.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for reliable data transmission?
quiz.why: The transport layer (where TCP lives) makes sure all data arrives, in order, and resends anything lost.

quiz.q: Which port number is normally used by HTTP?
quiz.why: Web traffic (HTTP) uses port 80. Ports 20/21 are for FTP and 110 is for POP3 email.

quiz.q: Which of the following is/are NOT a valid IP address?
quiz.why: Each of the four numbers in an IPv4 address must be between 0 and 255. In (d), 296 is too big. All the others stay within 0–255.

quiz.q: In IPv6, the number of bits used in an IP address is ____.
quiz.why: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. That makes far more addresses possible.

quiz.q: Which command(s) can check the reachability of one system from another?
quiz.why: ping sends a small "are you there?" message and waits for a reply. ls lists files and mkdir makes a folder.

quiz.q: Which network covers a small area like a room or building?
quiz.why: LAN = local (a room or building), MAN = metropolitan (a city), WAN = wide (countries; the internet is the biggest WAN).

quiz.q: Which of the following belong to the CIA Triad in information security?
quiz.why:
The CIA Triad is the three basic goals of security:

  • Confidentiality: only the right people can read it (your bank balance is private).
  • Integrity: nobody can secretly change it (no one edits your balance).
  • Availability: it works when you need it (the bank app isn't down).

The other options are real security ideas but are not part of the triad.

quiz.q: Which penetration testing model gives the tester no prior information about the target network?
quiz.why: Picture a box you can or can't see into. Black box = you see nothing and start blind, like a real outside attacker. White box = you get full details. Gray box = partial details. "Blue box" isn't a testing model.

quiz.q: Which statement(s) are true for packet-switched networks?
quiz.why: Packet switching is like the postal system. Your message is cut into small envelopes (packets) that share the same roads as everyone else's mail. The opposite, circuit switching, is like an old phone call: a dedicated line reserved just for you (options a, c, d). Packets can get delayed or lost, so (f) is false.
options: Bandwidth is dedicated for the entire session
Multiple connections can share the same link
Delay is always constant regardless of load
Requires end-to-end circuit setup before data transfer
Data is divided into smaller packets before transmission

quiz.q: Which OSI layer handles framing, MAC addressing, and error detection over a physical link?
quiz.why: The data link layer (layer 2) packs bits into "frames" and uses MAC addresses (hardware IDs) to deliver between two directly connected devices. The physical layer just sends raw 1s and 0s; the network layer handles IP addresses and routing.

quiz.q: A 1500-byte packet is sent over a 100 Kbps link with 8 ms propagation delay. When does it reach the destination (in ms)? (1K = 1000)
quiz.why:
Total time = time to push the bits onto the wire + time to travel.

  1. Convert to bits: 1500 bytes × 8 = 12,000 bits.
  2. Push time (transmission): 12,000 ÷ 100,000 bits/sec = 0.12 s = 120 ms.
  3. Travel time (propagation): 8 ms.
  4. Total: 120 + 8 = 128 ms.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of an IP address?
quiz.why: An IP address is a device's address on a network, so data can be routed to the right place, like a house address for mail.
options: Uniquely identifies a host or interface on a network
Specifies the number of open ports

quiz.q: What is the minimum size (in bytes) of a TCP header without options?
quiz.why: Every TCP packet carries a "label" (header) with info like port numbers. With no extras it is 20 bytes; with options it can grow up to 60 bytes.

quiz.q: Which IP header field is decremented at every router hop, to stop packets looping forever?
quiz.why: TTL is a countdown. Every router the packet passes through subtracts 1, and at 0 the packet is thrown away. That way a lost packet can't circle the internet forever.

quiz.q: If the IP header is 224 bits long, what is the value of the HLEN field (in decimal)?
quiz.why: HLEN doesn't store the length directly. It counts in chunks of 32 bits (4 bytes). So 224 ÷ 32 = 7.

quiz.q: How many bits are used to represent a MAC address?
quiz.why: A MAC address is the permanent hardware ID of a network card. It is 48 bits, usually written as 12 hex digits like 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.

quiz.q: An IP packet arrives with the first eight bits 0100 0101. How many bytes are in the OPTIONS field?
quiz.why:
Split the 8 bits into two halves.

  1. First half 0100 = 4, meaning IP version 4.
  2. Second half 0101 = 5. This is HLEN, counted in 4-byte chunks: 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.
  3. 20 bytes is the smallest possible IP header, so there is no room left for options: 20 − 20 = 0.

quiz.q: Which is/are true for TCP header flag bits?
quiz.why:
TCP flags are on/off switches in the packet label. Starting a connection is like a phone greeting:

  • SYN ("hello, can we talk?") = request (a)
  • SYN + ACK ("yes, I hear you") = confirmation (b)
  • URG = this part is urgent (e)

The trap: FIN is the polite goodbye, and RST is slamming the phone down. Options (c) and (d) swap them.
options: SYN=1, ACK=0 indicates a connection request
FIN is used to reject a connection
RST is used to gracefully terminate a connection

quiz.q: Which is a valid broadcast address for its subnet?
quiz.why:
A broadcast address means "send to everyone on this network". You get it by setting all the host part to the maximum (255s).

  • The /number says how many bits are the network part; the rest is the host part.
  • /8 → last three numbers are host → 10.255.255.255 (a is correct).
  • /24 → last number is host → 192.168.5.255 (c is correct).
  • (b) and (e) end in zeros: that's the network address (the name of the network), not broadcast.
  • (d) for /16 should be 172.16.255.255.

quiz.q: A packet arrives with D flag = 0, M flag = 0, offset = 5. Which is true?
quiz.why:
Big packets can be chopped into pieces (fragments).

  • M = 0 ("More fragments" = no) means nothing comes after this piece.
  • Offset = 5 (not 0) means this piece isn't at the start, so the packet was chopped.

Not first, nothing after it, so it's the last piece.
options: The packet has not been fragmented
The packet is the first fragment
The packet is the last fragment of a fragmented packet
The packet will be dropped due to invalid flags

quiz.q: Which IP address ranges are reserved for private use?
quiz.why: Private addresses are for inside homes and offices and never appear on the public internet (your home Wi-Fi probably uses 192.168.x.x). Memorise the three ranges: 10.x, 172.16–172.31, 192.168.x. The others are special-purpose: 169.254 is the address a computer gives itself when it can't get one, 224–239 is multicast, and 100.64 is for ISPs.

quiz.q: Which well-known ports are correctly matched with their service?
quiz.why:
The correct pairs to memorise:

ServicePortWhat it does
FTP21File transfer
SSH22Secure remote login
Telnet23Old, insecure remote login
SMTP25Sending email
DNS53Turns names (google.com) into IP addresses
HTTP80Web pages

Options c–f shuffle these numbers.

quiz.q: What subnet mask corresponds to CIDR /26?
quiz.why:
/26 means 26 ones, then zeros, out of 32 bits.

  1. The first 24 ones fill three numbers: 255.255.255.
  2. That leaves 2 more ones in the last number: 11000000.
  3. 11000000 = 128 + 64 = 192, giving 255.255.255.192.

Quick table: /25 = 128, /26 = 192, /27 = 224, /28 = 240.

quiz.q: Which statements about IPv4 fragmentation and the "Don't Fragment" (DF) bit are true?
quiz.why: MTU is the biggest packet a link can carry. DF = 1 is a "do not cut me" sticker. If the packet is too big and can't be cut, the router throws it away and sends back an error (a). With DF = 0 the router may cut it (c). DF lives in the Flags field, not the offset, and it never guarantees delivery.
options: If DF = 1 and the packet exceeds the MTU, it is dropped and an error is generated
If DF = 1, the router fragments the packet regardless
If DF = 0, fragmentation is allowed if needed
DF is part of the Fragment Offset field

quiz.q: A packet has HLEN = 12 and TOTAL LENGTH = 900 bytes. How many data bytes does it carry?
quiz.why:
1. HLEN counts 4-byte chunks: header = 12 × 4 = 48 bytes.
  2. Data = total − header = 900 − 48 = 852 bytes.

quiz.q: What is the size (in bytes) of a UDP header?
quiz.why: UDP is the simple, no-frills protocol. Its header has just 4 fields (source port, destination port, length, checksum) of 2 bytes each: 4 × 2 = 8 bytes. Compare TCP's minimum of 20.

quiz.q: Which is/are true about the connectionless routing used by IP?
quiz.why: "Connectionless" means no route is booked in advance. Each packet is like a separate letter: every post office (router) decides on the spot where to send it next. So two letters from the same sender can travel different roads.
options: Each packet is treated as an independent unit for routing
A fixed path is set up before any packet is sent
Packets between the same source and destination may take different paths

quiz.q: Which is/are FALSE about direct and indirect delivery?
quiz.why: Direct delivery is handing a note to someone in the same room: no router needed. That makes (c) false. Indirect delivery goes through routers until it reaches the destination's network. The final router then hands it over directly, which is why (e) is true.
options: Direct delivery happens when sender and destination are on the same physical network
Indirect delivery happens when the destination is on a different network
In direct delivery, packets always pass through at least one router
In indirect delivery, the packet is routed hop by hop to a router on the destination's network
Direct delivery can happen between the last router and the destination host

quiz.q: Which routing table flag says a route is for a single host rather than a whole network?
quiz.why: H = Host: the route points to one specific computer. Other common flags: U = route is Up, G = goes through a Gateway (router).

quiz.q: In OSPF, which packet type checks whether a neighbouring router is alive?
quiz.why: OSPF routers regularly send each other a "Hello". If a neighbour stops saying hello for a while, it's treated as down. It works like a check-in call.

quiz.q: Which address type delivers a packet to every host on a specific network?
quiz.why:
• Unicast = to one person.
  • Broadcast = to everyone on the network, like a loudspeaker announcement.
  • Anycast = to the nearest one of a group.

quiz.q: Which is/are FALSE about routing protocols?
quiz.why:
An autonomous system (AS) is one organisation's network, such as an ISP. There are two kinds of protocol:

  • Inside one AS (interior): RIP and OSPF.
  • Between ASes (exterior): BGP, the protocol that glues the internet together.

Options (c) and (e) swap these roles, so they're false. (a), (b) and (d) are correct facts.
options: RIP uses distance vector routing and can suffer from count-to-infinity
BGP is used for routing within a single autonomous system
OSPF uses Dijkstra's algorithm for shortest paths
RIP is typically used between different autonomous systems

quiz.q: What address represents the default route in an IPv4 routing table?
quiz.why: The default route is the "if nothing else matches, send it here" rule. It's written 0.0.0.0/0, meaning "any address". For comparison, 127.0.0.1 means "this computer itself" and 255.255.255.255 is a broadcast.

quiz.q: Which is/are FALSE about IPv6?
quiz.why: IPv6 dropped the old Class A/B/C system, so (a) is false. Its base header is a fixed 40 bytes; the 20–60 byte range describes IPv4, so (d) is false. (b) is true, e.g. 2001:db8::1. (c) is true: in IPv6 only the sender may split packets.
options: IPv6 has address classes like IPv4 (Class A, B, C)
IPv6 addresses are written in hexadecimal, separated by colons
IPv6 removes the need for routers along the way to fragment packets
The IPv6 base header is variable, from 20 to 60 bytes

quiz.q: How many bits are used for Hop Limit in the IPv6 base header?
quiz.why: Hop Limit is IPv6's version of TTL: a countdown reduced by 1 at each router. It is 8 bits, so it can count up to 255.

quiz.q: An organisation is given the block 172.20.64.0/20. How many valid host addresses does it have?
quiz.why:
1. An IPv4 address has 32 bits. /20 uses 20 for the network, leaving 32 − 20 = 12 bits for hosts.
  2. 12 bits give 2¹² = 4096 addresses.
  3. Two can't be given to devices: the network address (all zeros) and the broadcast address (all ones).
  4. 4096 − 2 = 4094.

General formula: usable hosts = 232 − prefix − 2.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a hypervisor in a pen-testing lab?
quiz.why: A virtual machine (VM) is a pretend computer running inside your real one. The hypervisor (e.g. VirtualBox) is the software that creates and runs them. This lets you build a safe practice lab, with an attacker VM and a victim VM, on one laptop.
options: Encrypts all traffic between virtual machines
Lets you create and manage multiple virtual machines on one physical computer
A hack-proof security layer for the host OS

quiz.q: Which information can a Whois lookup typically NOT give you?
quiz.why: Whois is the public register of who owns a domain name: owner, contacts, name servers, expiry date. Old copies of a website come from a different service, the Wayback Machine at archive.org.

quiz.q: How does host discovery with an ICMP Echo sweep work?
quiz.why: This is just ping sent to many addresses. Type 8 = Echo Request ("are you there?"), type 0 = Echo Reply ("yes!"). A reply means the computer is switched on.
options: An ICMP type-8 request is sent and an ICMP type-0 reply confirms the host is alive
A TCP SYN is sent and an ACK confirms the host is alive
ARP requests are broadcast to find all hosts

quiz.q: Which NMAP option(s) perform a TCP-based host discovery sweep?
quiz.why:
NMAP's -P? options are different ways to check if a host is alive. The letter after P tells you the method:

OptionSendsType
-PSTCP SYNTCP
-PATCP ACKTCP
-PEICMP EchoICMP
-PMICMP netMaskICMP
-PUUDPUDP

Only -PS and -PA use TCP.

quiz.q: In the TCP three-way handshake, what does the client send first?
quiz.why:
The handshake is three steps:

  1. Client: SYN ("can we talk?")
  2. Server: SYN-ACK ("yes, can you hear me?")
  3. Client: ACK ("yes, let's go")

quiz.q: In a TCP SYN (stealth) scan, which responses mean a port is open or closed?
quiz.why:
NMAP sends only step 1 of the handshake (SYN):

  • If the port answers SYN-ACK, someone is listening: open.
  • If it answers RST ("go away"), nobody is there: closed.

NMAP then never finishes the handshake. That's why it's called "stealth" or a "half-open" scan.

quiz.q: Which is/are true about VirtualBox's default networking mode (NAT)?
quiz.why: NAT works like your home router. The VMs sit behind the host computer with a private address (VirtualBox gives each one the same default, 10.0.2.15). They can reach out to the internet, but outsiders can't reach in directly.
options: Gives each VM a unique public IP
Gives guest machines the same private/virtual IP address
VMs in this mode can access the internet
Gives guests the host's own IP
VMs in NAT mode are reachable from outside by default

quiz.q: Which NMAP option(s) detect the operating system and/or service versions?
quiz.why:
• -O guesses the Operating system.
  • -sV finds service Versions (e.g. "Apache 2.4").
  • -A is "aggressive" or "all": OS detection, version detection, scripts and traceroute together.
  • -sn only checks if hosts are up (no port scan), and -Pn skips that check. Neither detects OS or versions.

(The solution PDF prints b, c and e without the dash; they are -O, -sV and -A.)

quiz.q: Ports 80 and 443 are open on a target. What can you infer?
quiz.why: Port 80 = HTTP (web) and port 443 = HTTPS (secure web). Both open means it's almost certainly a web server. SSH would be 22, email 25/110/143, DNS 53.
options: The target is very likely running SSH services
The target is very likely hosting a website (HTTP/HTTPS)
The target is running a mail server
The target is running a DNS resolver

quiz.q: Using --reason with a SYN scan, the reason field shows "syn-ack". What does that mean?
quiz.why: --reason makes NMAP explain each verdict. "syn-ack" means the target answered the knock with SYN-ACK, which (as in Q6) means the port is open.
options: The port is open because NMAP got a SYN-ACK from the target
The port is closed and there's no evidence

quiz.q: Which NMAP option(s) can trigger NMAP scripts to run?
quiz.why: NMAP has a library of add-on scripts (the NSE, NMAP Scripting Engine) that run extra checks. -sC runs the default scripts and is the same as --script=default. -A ("all") includes scripts too. -Pn and -sn only deal with whether a host is up.

quiz.q: Which tool(s) CANNOT be used for vulnerability scanning?
quiz.why:
Know each tool's job:

ToolWhat it does
Nessus, NexposeVulnerability scanners: list a system's known weaknesses
NMAPPort scanner; can also find vulnerabilities with scripts
HydraPassword guesser: tries many logins
CrunchWordlist maker: creates lists of possible passwords

Hydra and Crunch are password tools, not scanners.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common password cracking approach?
quiz.why:
• Dictionary = try a list of common words.
  • Brute force = try every possible combination.
  • Rule-based = try words with tweaks, like "password" → "P@ssw0rd1".
  • Shoulder surfing = literally watch someone type.

Packet sniffing just records network traffic. It may capture a password, but it isn't a cracking method.

quiz.q: Which TCP/IP protocol is connectionless and unreliable?
quiz.why: UDP fires data off without setting up a connection or checking it arrived, like shouting across a room. It's fast but things can get lost, so it's used for video calls and games. TCP is like a recorded-delivery letter, and FTP and Telnet run on TCP.

quiz.q: Which tool is mainly used to generate custom wordlists for dictionary attacks?
quiz.why: Crunch builds the list of guesses, e.g. "all 6-letter lowercase words". Hydra then uses a list to try logins, and Hashcat cracks stolen password hashes.

quiz.q: Which is/are FALSE about malware?
quiz.why: "All" is the trap. Viruses and worms copy themselves, but a Trojan doesn't. It just pretends to be a useful program, like the wooden horse, and waits for you to run it.
options: All malware types can copy themselves (self-replicate)
Malware can give an attacker partial or full control of a system
Malware can arrive via file sharing or fake/pirated software
Malware can modify, corrupt or delete data

quiz.q: In a MAC flooding attack, what is the goal of overwhelming a switch's CAM table?
quiz.why: A switch keeps a table (the CAM table) of which device is plugged into which port, so it sends data only where it belongs. The attacker floods it with thousands of fake entries until it's full. A confused switch falls back to sending everything to everyone, like a hub, so the attacker can now eavesdrop on traffic.
options: Force the switch to act like a hub, sending traffic to all ports

quiz.q: Which NMAP script identifies the operating system of an SMB-enabled target?
quiz.why: SMB is the Windows file-sharing service. Script names describe what they do: os-discovery finds the OS, brute guesses passwords, enum-users lists user accounts. http-os-brute isn't a real script.

quiz.q: Hydra runs a dictionary attack on SSH, testing 5000 passwords against 4 usernames. What is the maximum number of login attempts?
quiz.why: Every password is tried with every username: 4 × 5000 = 20,000 attempts in the worst case.

quiz.q: A brute-force cracker must try every 4-character password made of lowercase letters (26 options per position). How many combinations are there?
quiz.why: Each of the 4 positions has 26 choices, so multiply: 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 = 26⁴ = 456,976. Each extra character multiplies the work by 26, which is why longer passwords are much safer.

quiz.q: Which attack involves pretending to be a legitimate entity to gain access?
quiz.why:
To masquerade = to wear a disguise. The attacker pretends to be someone trusted.

  • Replay = recording a real message and re-sending it later.
  • Modification = changing a message on its way.
  • Traffic analysis = just watching who talks to whom.

quiz.q: Encrypt "SECURE" with a shift cipher, k = 3 (wrap Z → A).
quiz.why:
This is the Caesar cipher: move each letter 3 places forward in the alphabet.

PlainSECURE
+3VHFXUH

Result: VHFXUH.

quiz.q: A mono-alphabetic cipher maps A–Z to Q W E R T Y U I O P A S D F G H J K L Z X C V B N M. Encrypt "CODE".
quiz.why:
Line up the alphabet with the key (it's the keyboard's QWERTY rows) and swap each letter.

  • C is the 3rd letter → 3rd key letter is E
  • O is the 15th → G
  • D is the 4th → R
  • E is the 5th → T

Result: EGRT.

quiz.q: Which is/are FALSE about hashing algorithms for message integrity?
quiz.why:
A hash is a one-way fingerprint. You can make a fingerprint from a person, but you can't rebuild the person from it. So (c) is false. The rest are true:

  • (a) No two messages should share a hash (a "collision").
  • (b) The same message always gives the same hash.
  • (d) Change one letter and the whole hash changes (the "avalanche effect").
options: A good hash should resist collisions
The same input always gives the same hash
A hash can be reversed to get the original message
A tiny change in input gives a very different hash

quiz.q: Decrypt "KHOOR" (shift cipher, k = 3).
quiz.why: To decrypt, move each letter 3 places back: K→H, H→E, O→L, O→L, R→O = HELLO.

quiz.q: A DoS attack makes a service unavailable to real users. Which category is this?
quiz.why:
The four classic categories, each hitting one security goal:

CategoryWhat happensGoal attacked
InterruptionService is blocked or brokenAvailability
InterceptionSomeone secretly reads the dataConfidentiality
ModificationData is changed on the wayIntegrity
FabricationFake data is createdAuthenticity

DoS = blocking the service = interruption.

quiz.q: With public-key cryptography, A wants to send B a confidential message. Which key encrypts it?
quiz.why: A locks the box with B's open padlock (B's public key). Only B has the key that opens it (B's private key), so only B can read it.

quiz.q: What block size (in bits) does DES use for plaintext?
quiz.why: DES encrypts data in chunks of 64 bits. Don't mix it up with the key: DES's key is 56 bits (stored as 64 with 8 check bits).

quiz.q: 150 parties communicate using public-key encryption (like RSA). How many distinct keys are needed?
quiz.why: Each person needs just one pair (1 public + 1 private), whoever they talk to. 150 people × 2 keys = 300.

quiz.q: 40 parties communicate using symmetric-key encryption. How many distinct keys are needed?
quiz.why:
With symmetric keys, every pair of people needs its own shared secret. Count the pairs:

(N(N-1)) / (2) = (40 × 39) / (2) = 780

That fast growth is the big weakness of symmetric keys, and why public-key cryptography is useful (compare Q9).

quiz.q: A message M is hashed to H = HASH(M). Which is/are true?
quiz.why: Whether you hash one word or a whole movie file, SHA-256 always gives exactly 256 bits. So the hash is fixed-length and usually much smaller than the message.
options: H usually has far fewer bits than M
H and M always have exactly the same number of bits
Hashing gives a fixed-length output whatever the input size
Output length grows with input length

quiz.q: Which is/are true?
quiz.why: Check each against the table above. DES's key is 56 bits, not 128. SHA-256's number is its output size (256). Triple DES tops out at 168 bits.
options: Triple DES uses a fixed 512-bit key

quiz.q: Which is/are true about SSL/TLS?
quiz.why: HTTPS is just HTTP (web pages) wrapped in TLS encryption: that's the padlock in your browser. Encryption adds work, so it's not faster (b). It runs high up the stack, not at the physical (cables) layer (c). It doesn't give non-repudiation (d).
options: HTTPS relies on SSL/TLS to secure HTTP
SSL/TLS makes data travel faster than plain HTTP
TLS works at the physical layer
The SSL Record Protocol guarantees non-repudiation

quiz.q: Which is/are true about collision resistance in hash functions?
quiz.why: A "collision" is two different messages with the same fingerprint. Collision resistance means finding any such pair should be practically impossible. That's the definition, so (b). It's a strong requirement, and has nothing to do with keeping data secret.
options: It's a weaker requirement than second preimage resistance
It should be computationally hard to find any two different messages with the same hash
It applies only to keyed hashes (MACs)

quiz.q: Which is/are true about verifying a digital signature?
quiz.why: A digital signature is the reverse of encryption. The signer "locks" with their private key, which only they have, and anyone can check it with their public key. If it checks out, you know who signed it and that nothing changed. The signer doesn't need to be around.
options: The verifier uses the signer's public key
The verifier uses the signer's private key
Successful verification shows the message wasn't altered and came from the claimed signer
The signer must be online during verification

quiz.q: Which property of digital signatures stops the signer from later denying they signed?
quiz.why: "Repudiate" means to deny. Only the signer holds their private key, so they can't later claim "that wasn't me". It works like a handwritten signature on a contract.

quiz.q: Which statement is FALSE about keyed vs unkeyed hash functions?
quiz.why: Anyone can compute an unkeyed hash such as SHA-256. An attacker could change the message and simply recompute the hash, so it proves nothing about who sent it. A keyed hash (HMAC) mixes in a secret key, so only key holders can produce it.
options: An unkeyed hash can verify integrity if the hash comes from a trusted source
A keyed hash needs a secret key to compute
An unkeyed hash inherently provides authenticity
HMAC gives both integrity and some authentication

quiz.q: Which IPSec mode protects only the payload and keeps the original IP header intact?
quiz.why:
IPSec secures IP packets.

  • Transport mode encrypts the letter but leaves the envelope's address visible.
  • Tunnel mode puts the whole envelope, address and all, inside a new sealed envelope. This is how VPNs work.

"Replay" and "Confidential" modes don't exist.

quiz.q: What digest size (in bits) does MD5 produce?
quiz.why: MD5 always outputs 128 bits. It is now considered broken for security use, but the number is still examinable.

quiz.q: What block size (in bits) does SHA-512 use?
quiz.why: Careful, this is the block size, not the output. SHA-512 chews through input 1024 bits at a time and outputs a 512-bit hash.

quiz.q: Which best describes steganography?
quiz.why: Encryption makes a message unreadable; steganography makes it invisible. The message is hidden inside something innocent-looking, like a photo, so nobody even knows it exists. Think of invisible ink on an ordinary letter.
options: Encrypting with public and private keys
Embedding information inside another cover medium

quiz.q: Which are valid examples of steganography?
quiz.why: All three hide data inside a "cover" file (image, audio, program). (c) is encryption and (e) is a signature: neither hides that a message exists.
options: Hiding data inside an audio clip
Encrypting a file so only the recipient can decrypt it
Hiding data inside an executable file

quiz.q: Which are examples of behavioural biometrics?
quiz.why:
Biometrics identify you by your body. There are two kinds:

  • Behavioural = how you do things: how you sign (speed, pressure), how you walk (gait), how you type (rhythm).
  • Physiological = what you are: fingerprint, iris, retina, face shape.

quiz.q: Which biometric is generally considered to give very high uniqueness and reliability?
quiz.why: The coloured ring of your eye (the iris) has an extremely detailed pattern that is unique to each person and barely changes over life. Voice, face, signature and walk all vary with mood, age, illness or lighting.

quiz.q: What is a Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack?
quiz.why: DoS = overwhelming a service so real users can't use it, like 10,000 prank callers jamming a pizza shop's phone line. Nothing has to be stolen or deleted.
options: Prevents legitimate users from accessing a service

quiz.q: How does a Smurf DoS attack typically work?
quiz.why:
1. The attacker sends a "ping everyone" message to a whole network (the broadcast address).
  2. They fake the sender address to be the victim's.
  3. Every computer on that network replies, all to the victim, at once.

It's like sending a party invitation to 500 people with your enemy's phone number for RSVPs. Oversized packets (a) is a different attack, the "Ping of Death".
options: Sends oversized IP packets to crash the target
Sends fake ICMP Echo requests to a network's broadcast address with the victim's IP as the sender, so many hosts flood the victim with replies
Exploits a buffer overflow in a web server
Uses SQL injection on a database

quiz.q: Which attack abuses the TCP three-way handshake by leaving connections half-open?
quiz.why: Recall the handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. In a SYN flood the attacker sends thousands of SYNs but never sends the final ACK. The server keeps a slot open for each half-finished connection until it runs out, and real users get refused.

quiz.q: What does PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) mainly provide for secure email?
quiz.why: PGP signs emails (proving who sent them) and encrypts them (keeping them private). It uses the hashing and public/private keys from Weeks 6–7. It can't guarantee delivery and has nothing to do with spam.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of DNS?
quiz.why: DNS is the internet's phone book. You type google.com, and DNS looks up the number (IP address) your computer actually needs to connect.
options: Translating human-readable domain names into IP addresses

quiz.q: A grayscale image is 1500 × 1200 pixels, 8 bits per pixel. With LSB steganography (1 hidden bit per pixel), how many bytes can be hidden?
quiz.why:
LSB = Least Significant Bit. Changing the last bit of a pixel alters its shade so slightly the eye can't see it, so you can hide 1 bit per pixel.

  1. Pixels: 1500 × 1200 = 1,800,000, so 1,800,000 hidden bits.
  2. Bits to bytes: 1,800,000 ÷ 8 = 225,000 bytes.

(The "8 bits per pixel" is a distractor; only 1 of those 8 is used.)

quiz.q: Which is/are true for sniffing?
quiz.why: Sniffing = capturing and reading traffic. Normally a network card ignores data meant for other computers. Promiscuous mode turns that filter off so it keeps everything. Finding vulnerabilities and listing users are different techniques.
options: Analysing network activity by capturing traffic
May require the network card to be in promiscuous mode to capture frames not addressed to it

quiz.q: Which is/are NOT features of Wireshark?
quiz.why: Wireshark is a watcher: it captures, displays, filters and summarises traffic. It doesn't change traffic, and it's not an attack tool like SQL injection.
options: Showing packet details in a GUI

quiz.q: Which protocols are vulnerable to sniffing?
quiz.why: HTTP, FTP and Telnet send everything in plain text, passwords included, like a postcard anyone can read. HTTPS, SSL and SSH encrypt the data, so a sniffer only sees gibberish. Easy rule: the "S" usually means Secure.

quiz.q: Which feature(s) are NOT in the Ettercap tool?
quiz.why: Ettercap is a man-in-the-middle tool: it sits between two computers and can watch, filter, drop or inject into their traffic. SQL injection (sqlmap's job) and password cracking (Hydra's job) belong to other tools.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a human-based social engineering attack?
quiz.why:
Social engineering = tricking people, not computers. There are two kinds:

  • Human-based (in person): pretending to be IT staff (impersonation), peeking at someone typing (shoulder surfing), following someone through a locked door (tailgating).
  • Computer-based (through a screen): phishing emails, fake pop-ups.

quiz.q: A DoS attack that abuses the TCP handshake by leaving connections incomplete is called:
quiz.why: Same idea as Week 8 Q7: thousands of "hello" (SYN) messages, never followed by the final ACK, fill up the server's waiting list.

quiz.q: Which tool causes DoS by sending partial HTTP requests and never finishing them?
quiz.why: Slowloris (named after a slow animal) opens many connections to a web server and sends each request very slowly, never finishing. The server politely waits on all of them until it has no connections left for real visitors.

quiz.q: Which mode lets a network card capture frames not addressed to it?
quiz.why: Promiscuous mode (see Q1) means the card accepts all traffic it sees. Don't confuse it with monitor mode, which is a Wi-Fi-specific mode for listening to wireless signals.

quiz.q: Which are computer-based social engineering attacks?
quiz.why: If it arrives on a screen (email, pop-up, chain letter), it's computer-based. Shoulder surfing and tailgating need you physically there, so they're human-based (see Q5).

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of ARP spoofing in a sniffing attack?
quiz.why: ARP is how computers on a local network find each other's hardware (MAC) address from an IP address. The attacker sends fake ARP replies saying "I'm the router". Now the victim's traffic goes to the attacker first, who reads it and passes it on. That's a man-in-the-middle attack.
options: Redirect traffic between two hosts through the attacker's machine
Permanently disable the target's network card

quiz.q: Which are hardware-based attacks?
quiz.why: Both need the physical device: probing touches the chip's wires, and EM analysis measures the radio signals it leaks. SQL injection and XSS attack websites, and phishing attacks people.

quiz.q: Which is/are true about side-channel attacks?
quiz.why: The maths can be perfect; the leak is in the real device running it, so (a) is true and (e) false. To measure power or radio noise you usually need to be near or touching the device (b), using clues like timing or power (d). (c) is false: side channels use extra information beyond inputs and outputs.
options: They exploit weaknesses in how an algorithm is implemented, not the algorithm itself
They may need physical access to, or closeness to, the device
They rely only on analysing input/output pairs
They can use timing, power consumption or electromagnetic emissions
They exploit mathematical weaknesses in the algorithm's design

quiz.q: Computing x²² with the square-and-multiply method, how many squarings and multiplications are needed?
quiz.why:
Write the power in binary: 22 = 10110 (5 bits, three 1s).

  • Squarings = number of bits − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4
  • Multiplications = number of 1s − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2

Step by step, reading the bits after the first: start x → bit 0: square = x² → bit 1: square + multiply = x⁵ → bit 1: square + multiply = x¹¹ → bit 0: square = x²². This matters for security because a multiply takes extra time and power, so watching a chip can reveal the secret bits.

quiz.q: Which is/are true about Differential Power Analysis (DPA) and Simple Power Analysis (SPA)?
quiz.why:
A "trace" is a recording of the chip's power use over time.

  • SPA (Simple) = look at one recording and spot the pattern by eye.
  • DPA (Differential) = collect many recordings and use statistics to tease out tiny differences invisible in any one. That makes it more powerful, so (d) is false.
options: DPA needs only one power trace
DPA needs many traces plus statistics
DPA uses statistics over many traces to reveal what single traces don't show
DPA is generally less effective than SPA
SPA directly reads patterns in one or a few traces

quiz.q: Which PUF property means the response y = PUF(x) to a challenge x can be computed efficiently?
quiz.why: "Evaluate" = work out the answer. Evaluability means getting the response is quick and easy. Unclonability = nobody can build a copy. One-wayness = you can't work backwards from y to x.

quiz.q: What does PUF stand for in hardware security?
quiz.why: Physically Unclonable Function. Tiny random flaws from manufacturing make every chip slightly different. A PUF uses those flaws as a built-in fingerprint that can't be copied, even by the factory.

quiz.q: What is a hardware Trojan?
quiz.why: It's a hidden extra circuit secretly added to a chip during design or manufacture. It sleeps until a trigger (a certain date or input), then does damage, such as leaking keys or shutting down. It is built into the hardware, not software.
options: A software virus targeting firmware updates
A malicious, deliberate change to a chip's circuitry that activates under specific trigger conditions
A testing tool used before shipping
A feature to make hardware faster under load

quiz.q: Which is/are true about hardware Trojans?
quiz.why: A Trojan is tiny on purpose, a few gates among billions, so it's hard to find (a). There's no single detection method that catches them all, and checking costs time and resources (c). They live in the circuit, not software, so (d) is false.
options: They usually add very little extra hardware, so they're hard to detect
One universal method easily detects them
Detecting them often adds extra design, testing or runtime cost
They're inserted only through software changes

quiz.q: Which hardware attack(s) are generally considered invasive?
quiz.why: Invasive = you physically open or damage the chip, e.g. removing its casing and placing needles on its wires (probing). The others just measure from outside without breaking anything.

quiz.q: Which software techniques help defend against timing side-channel attacks?
quiz.why: A timing attack works because some secrets make the code run faster or slower. The fix is to make it always take the same time, either with dummy work (a) or by writing constant-time code (d). Complexity alone (c) doesn't hide timing. Masking (b) protects against power leaks, not timing.
options: Adding dummy computations so every path takes the same time
Making the program more complex without fixing timing differences

quiz.q: Which Metasploit module takes advantage of a known vulnerability on the target?
quiz.why: The exploit is the key that opens the lock. The payload is what you do once the door is open.

quiz.q: Which command launches the Metasploit Framework console?
quiz.why: msfconsole = the Metasploit Framework console. msfvenom is a separate tool for building payloads. The other two don't exist.

quiz.q: Which Metasploit command shows which target operating systems an exploit works on?
quiz.why: In Metasploit, show lists things and set chooses a value. "Which systems can this exploit hit?" = show targets.

quiz.q: Which option sets the target's IP address?
quiz.why: RHOST = Remote host = the victim. LHOST is your own machine. The PORT versions set port numbers.

quiz.q: Which Meterpreter command retrieves stored password hashes from the target?
quiz.why: hashdump = dump (copy out) the password hashes, which you can then crack offline with Hashcat. The others: getuid = which user am I, getsystem = try to become admin, sysinfo = system details, ps = list running programs.

quiz.q: Which tool brute-forces hidden files and directories on a web server?
quiz.why: Dirb = directory buster. It tries thousands of common folder names (/admin, /backup, ...) to find pages the site doesn't link to.

quiz.q: If a page is vulnerable to error-based SQL injection, what happens with bad or malicious input?
quiz.why: "Error-based" says it all. The site shows the raw database error, and that error leaks clues (table names, query shape) the attacker uses for the next step.
options: It shows a database error message revealing the query structure
It redirects to a login page
It crashes the whole server permanently

quiz.q: Which SQLMAP option lists all database names on the target?
quiz.why: sqlmap automates SQL injection. Its options go from big to small: --dbs (all databases) → --tables (tables inside one) → --dump (copy out the actual data).

quiz.q: Which are recognised types of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
quiz.why:
XSS = sneaking the attacker's JavaScript into a web page so it runs in other visitors' browsers. The three real types:

  • Stored: the script is saved on the site, e.g. in a comment, and hits everyone who views it.
  • Reflected: the script is in a link; the page bounces it straight back to whoever clicks.
  • DOM-based: the page's own JavaScript inserts the attacker's input unsafely.

quiz.q: A login form runs: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'INPUT1' AND password = 'INPUT2'. Which username inputs are classic SQL injection attempts to bypass login?
quiz.why:
The website pastes your input straight into its database question. Normal input asks "is the username X and password Y?".

  • (b) The ' closes the username early, then OR '1'='1' adds a condition that is always true, so the check passes.
  • (d) Same trick, and -- marks the rest of the query (the password check) as a comment, so it's ignored.

(The solution PDF prints option d as 'OR 1=1 -, a lost dash; the standard payload is ' OR 1=1 --.) The fix for websites is to never paste user input directly into queries.

quiz.q: In an ICMP Echo sweep, the scanner gets an ICMP Type 0 reply to a Type 8 request. What does that mean?
quiz.why: Type 8 = "are you there?" (Echo Request), Type 0 = "yes!" (Echo Reply). A reply means the host is up. This is the same idea as Week 4 Q3.
options: The target host does not support ICMP

quiz.q: Which NMAP option(s) do a TCP-based sweep for host discovery?
quiz.why: This repeats Week 4 Q4. -PS (TCP SYN) and -PA (TCP ACK) use TCP. -PE and -PM use ICMP, and -PU uses UDP.

quiz.q: Which are automatically performed with NMAP's -sn option?
quiz.why: -sn checks which hosts are alive by default with a ping (ICMP Echo) plus TCP probes. It does not send UDP probes unless you ask.

quiz.q: Which NMAP option treats all hosts as online and skips host discovery?
quiz.why: -Pn = no ping. It's useful when a target blocks pings but is still really there, so NMAP goes straight to scanning its ports.

quiz.q: Statement (i): -sn does host discovery only, no port scan. Statement (ii): -Pn skips host discovery and goes straight to port scanning.
quiz.why: They're opposites, and both statements describe them correctly. -sn = "who's home?" only. -Pn = "assume they're home, check the doors".

quiz.q: Which is/are true about NMAP's -F (fast scan) option?
quiz.why: A normal NMAP scan checks the 1000 most common ports. -F checks only the top 100, so it's faster. That also makes (d) wrong: 1000 is the default, not -F.
options: Scans the top 100 most common ports
Faster than a default scan because it checks fewer ports

quiz.q: Which NMAP option does a UDP port scan?
quiz.why: -sU = UDP. All the others are TCP scans: T = connect, S = SYN, A = ACK, N = NULL.

quiz.q: Which scan completes the full TCP three-way handshake to find a port's state?
quiz.why: The Connect scan (-sT) makes a real, complete connection: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. The SYN scan stops halfway (Week 4 Q6). FIN, NULL and Xmas send odd flag combinations with no handshake at all.

quiz.q: How many ports does nmap --top-ports 20 target_ip scan?
quiz.why: --top-ports N scans exactly the N most common ports, so 20.

quiz.q: How many IP addresses are covered by nmap -sL 10.10.5.100-115?
quiz.why: Count from 100 to 115 including both ends: 115 − 100 + 1 = 16. A common mistake is answering 15 by forgetting the +1. (Strictly, -sL only lists the 16 targets without sending them anything.)
